Clinical performance is determined using prospectively collected capillary blood specimens, with HIV status established through a defined reference testing algorithm performed on matched plasma samples. The protocol also includes assessment of operational characteristics and ease of use to support decisions regarding suitability for use in settings with limited infrastructure. Acceptance criteria and responsibilities of WHO, manufacturers and performance evaluation laboratories are specified to ensure a transparent, consistent and scientifically rigorous prequalification process.

title: Department of Regulation and Prequalification: strategic action plan 2025-2028
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This strategic action plan outlines the priorities and objectives of the World Health Organization’s Department of Regulation and Prequalification (RPQ) for the period 2025–2028. The document describes WHO’s role in strengthening national and regional regulatory systems and expanding access to safe, effective and quality-assured health products, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Closely aligned with WHO’s Fourteenth General Programme of Work and the Access to Medicines and Health Products Division Road Map 2025–2030, the plan presents a framework to support universal health coverage, health emergency preparedness and equitable access to medicines, vaccines, diagnostics and medical devices.

The publication identifies five strategic priorities focused on strengthening regulatory systems, increasing preparedness for public health emergencies, expanding WHO prequalification and risk assessment pathways, improving regulatory support activities and optimizing operational performance. It addresses challenges related to regulatory capacity, substandard and falsified products, innovation, environmental sustainability and access inequities. The plan also emphasizes reliance mechanisms, regulatory convergence, quality management systems, pharmacovigilance, collaboration with national regulatory authorities and the development of more efficient and transparent regulatory and prequalification processes to improve public health outcomes globally.

abstract:
This guidance document provides instructions for manufacturers on the preparation and submission of product dossiers for the WHO prequalification assessment of in vitro diagnostic (IVD) medical devices. It aligns WHO dossier requirements with the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) Table of Contents format, promoting a harmonized structure for technical documentation while describing the evidence needed to demonstrate the quality, safety and performance of IVDs. The document is intended to support manufacturers in compiling complete, well-organized submissions and should be used together with the WHO Product Dossier Checklist and relevant Technical Specification Series documents.

The guidance describes the required administrative information, product description, analytical and clinical performance evidence, labelling, quality management system documentation, and supporting reference materials that manufacturers must provide. It specifies expectations for study design, risk management, stability, usability, clinical evaluation and conformity with the IMDRF Essential Principles, as well as formatting and submission requirements for electronic dossiers. The document emphasizes that complete, scientifically justified and clearly referenced documentation is essential to facilitate WHO assessment and to support decisions within the prequalification process.

title: [WHO list of international comparator products]
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This workbook provides the WHO List of International Comparator Products, a reference resource that supports the selection of comparator pharmaceutical products for equivalence assessment of interchangeable multisource (generic) medicines. Based on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, it identifies recommended finished pharmaceutical products, corresponding marketing authorization holders, and the markets where their quality, safety and efficacy are considered to be best documented. The resource also identifies comparator products recommended by the WHO Prequalification Team – Medicines (PQTm) and includes information compiled from publicly available sources, medicines regulatory authorities and manufacturers.

The workbook is intended to support medicines regulatory authorities, assessors, manufacturers and other stakeholders involved in the evaluation and registration of generic pharmaceutical products. It facilitates the consistent selection of appropriate comparator products in accordance with WHO regulatory guidance and related technical standards. In addition to the tabulated comparator list, the resource includes explanatory notes, definitions, references to relevant WHO Technical Report Series guidance and information on PQTm expressions of interest, providing a practical reference for implementing internationally harmonized approaches to pharmaceutical equivalence assessment.

title: Establishing stability of in vitro diagnostic medical devices
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This technical guidance document provides recommendations for establishing and verifying the stability of in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDs) within the framework of WHO prequalification. Intended for manufacturers of IVDs, it outlines principles, study designs and evidence requirements to support claims related to shelf-life, transport stability, component stability and in-use stability. The guidance emphasizes that stability is fundamental to ensuring reliable performance throughout the intended life of an IVD and that manufacturers must generate objective, scientifically sound evidence to substantiate all stability claims. It also explains the expectations of WHO prequalification, particularly for products intended for use in resource-limited settings and under diverse environmental conditions.

The document describes risk-based approaches to stability testing, including the selection of critical performance characteristics, environmental conditions, testing panels, production lots and statistical methods. It addresses the evaluation of shelf-life through real-time and accelerated studies, the impact of transportation and storage conditions, the stability of components and control materials, and the documentation required in study plans and reports. The guidance further highlights the importance of considering user environments in WHO Member States and ensuring that stability studies reflect actual conditions of transport, storage and use, thereby supporting the quality, safety and effectiveness of IVDs throughout their life-cycle.

It explains the role of risk management in ensuring the safety, quality and performance of IVDs throughout their entire life cycle, from product conception and design to manufacturing, commercialization and post-market activities. The guidance is aligned with internationally recognized standards, including ISO 14971 and ISO 13485, and is intended to support manufacturers in preparing product dossiers and demonstrating compliance during WHO prequalification assessments.

The publication describes key principles, responsibilities and processes for effective risk management, emphasizing its integration within quality management systems and its application across all organizational functions. It outlines approaches for hazard identification, risk analysis, evaluation, control and monitoring, and discusses commonly used tools such as failure mode and effects analysis. The document also addresses risk management considerations related to design control, verification and validation, performance studies, labelling, manufacturing processes, supplier management and change control. By promoting a systematic and documented approach to identifying and mitigating risks, the guidance supports the development and continued supply of safe, reliable and fit-for-purpose IVDs, including those intended for use in resource-limited settings.

The guidance addresses the specific challenges associated with the use of IVDs in resource-limited settings and by users with varying levels of technical expertise. It presents principles for readability, document design, use of graphics and job aids, document control, pre-testing and accessibility of IFUs.

The publication describes the essential content that should be included in an IFU, including product identification, intended use, warnings and precautions, specimen collection and handling, storage conditions, testing procedures, quality control measures, result interpretation, limitations and performance characteristics. It also provides recommendations on communicating analytical and clinical performance data and on tailoring information to professional users, lay users and self-testing contexts. title: WHO’s performance evaluation procedure for in vitro diagnostics
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
WHO’s performance evaluation of in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) establishes a standardized procedure to independently assess the performance and operational characteristics of diagnostic products, including their suitability for use in resource-limited settings, as a prerequisite for WHO prequalification. This normative document defines the scope, requirements and processes governing performance evaluation, positioning it as a distinct but essential step preceding prequalification assessment. It is intended primarily for manufacturers seeking to submit products for evaluation and provides a structured overview of eligibility criteria, submission requirements and procedural conditions.

The document details the full evaluation pathway, including submission and review of expressions of interest, commissioning modalities, roles of performance evaluation laboratories, and conditions for initiating and conducting evaluations. It describes the generation, review and ownership of evaluation results, as well as decision-making processes regarding successful completion. Key provisions address confidentiality, conflicts of interest, data sharing and publication of results, including public assessment reports used to inform procurement decisions. The procedure clarifies that evaluation outcomes inform, but do not guarantee, prequalification decisions, and outlines conditions for termination, withdrawal and financial responsibilities, ensuring transparency, consistency and integrity.

title: WHO certification scheme on the quality of pharmaceutical products
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This publication provides an overview of the World Health Organization (WHO) Certification Scheme on the quality of pharmaceutical products moving in international commerce, a voluntary regulatory reliance mechanism established in 1969 to support Member States in ensuring the quality, safety and efficacy of medicines circulating globally. The document describes the background, purpose and evolution of the Scheme, including successive revisions undertaken to address changes in pharmaceutical manufacturing, globalization, regulatory science and digitalization. It outlines the role of the Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CPP) within the broader regulatory ecosystem and discusses its relationship with other reliance tools and collaborative regulatory mechanisms.

The document also presents perspectives and implementation experiences from national and regional regulatory authorities and the pharmaceutical industry, highlighting challenges related to harmonization, administrative burden, legalization procedures and adoption of electronic certificates. Strengths and limitations of the Scheme are examined, including issues related to regulatory capacity and verification of compliance with good manufacturing practices. The document emphasizes the continued relevance of the Scheme, the importance of international cooperation and reliance practices, and the need to modernize regulatory processes to facilitate timely access to quality-assured medicines.

title: WHO guidelines for malaria, 14 March 2023

abstract:
The WHO Guidelines for malaria consolidate current WHO recommendations for malaria prevention, diagnosis, treatment, elimination and prevention of re-establishment into a single, evidence-based resource. Developed through WHO’s standardized guideline development process, the publication supports policy-makers, national malaria programmes and other stakeholders in adapting recommendations to local epidemiological and operational contexts. The guidelines are presented as “living guidelines”, enabling timely updates as new evidence becomes available, while linking recommendations to supporting evidence, evidence-to-decision frameworks and implementation resources.

The publication covers vector control interventions, preventive chemotherapies, malaria vaccination, case management and interventions for malaria elimination. It provides evidence-based recommendations on vector control tools, antimalarial medicines for preventive chemotherapy, vaccination strategies, and the diagnosis and treatment of uncomplicated and severe malaria across different population groups and settings. The document also outlines the role of WHO good practice statements, describes the intended use of recommendations in national policy development, and explains the relationship between guideline recommendations and the WHO prequalification process for diagnostics, medicines, vaccines and vector control products.

The report highlights challenges related to the development, testing, regulation and access to vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and emphasizes the importance of target product profiles, preferred product characteristics and coordinated priority-setting to guide innovation.

The document also examines the role of PDPs, WHO and funders in advancing health technology development, strengthening clinical research capacity, supporting local manufacturing and fostering sustainable R&D ecosystems. Discussions addressed regulatory pathways, WHO prequalification and guideline processes, funding constraints, capacity-building, technology transfer and collaboration mechanisms. title: Thermostability of human insulin
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This technical brief examines the thermostability of human insulin and its implications for improving access to diabetes treatment, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where reliable refrigeration may be limited. Against the backdrop of the growing global burden of diabetes and persistent barriers to insulin affordability and availability, the document reviews evidence on the effects of temperature on insulin stability and summarizes current knowledge regarding storage conditions beyond manufacturers’ recommended ranges. It highlights the importance of human insulin as an essential medicine and the need to ensure its effective use in diverse climatic and resource-constrained settings.

Drawing on published studies and previously unpublished manufacturer data, the brief finds that human insulin generally maintains clinically relevant potency under a range of elevated temperature conditions. It also outlines WHO prequalification pathways and regulatory considerations for updating storage recommendations based on stability data. The document emphasizes the role of stability studies in supporting quality-assured insulin products and discusses how revised storage conditions could facilitate access in settings where cold-chain management is challenging. It concludes that further research, data sharing and regulatory engagement are needed to support more practical storage guidance and enhance the availability and affordability of human insulin worldwide.

title: Expedited research and approval of medicines for drug-resistant bacterial infections in children
authors: Williams, PC; Noel, GJ; Nambiar, S; O'Brien, S; Paterson, DL; Bielicki, JA; Sharland, M; Bradley, JS
abstract:
Multidrug-resistant bacterial infections are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality in neonates, infants and children, yet access to new antibacterial therapies for paediatric patients continues to lag several years behind adult approval. This policy and practice article examines the regulatory, scientific and operational barriers responsible for these delays and proposes strategies to accelerate the development, evaluation and approval of antibacterial medicines for children. Particular attention is given to the unmet needs of neonates and young infants and to the challenges faced by low- and middle-income countries.

The authors advocate more efficient paediatric drug development pathways based on pharmacokinetic studies, appropriate extrapolation of adult safety and efficacy data, simultaneous investigation across paediatric age groups where justified, inclusion of adolescents in adult clinical trials, streamlined conditional approval pathways and the use of real-world evidence to complement clinical trial data. Additional recommendations include harmonizing regulatory requirements, strengthening international paediatric clinical trial networks, standardizing protocols and contracts, engaging community stakeholders and increasing sustainable funding. These measures aim to ensure earlier access to safe, effective antibacterial therapies while maintaining rigorous safety oversight and supporting equitable global access for children with multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.

title: Regulatory considerations on artificial intelligence for health
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This publication provides a high-level overview of key regulatory considerations for the safe and appropriate development, evaluation, deployment and oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) systems for health. Developed through the WHO–International Telecommunication Union Focus Group on AI for Health Working Group on Regulatory Considerations, it is intended as a resource for developers, regulators, policy-makers, manufacturers and health practitioners rather than as a regulatory framework or formal guidance. The document examines six principal topic areas: documentation and transparency; risk management across the total product lifecycle; intended use and analytical and clinical validation; data quality; privacy and data protection; and engagement and collaboration.

The publication emphasizes that trustworthy AI for health requires transparent documentation, proportionate risk management, rigorous validation, high-quality data, protection of privacy and continuous collaboration among stakeholders throughout the AI system lifecycle. It highlights the importance of post-market monitoring, quality management, cybersecurity, and adaptation to diverse health-care settings while recognizing the rapid evolution of AI technologies. The report concludes by encouraging continued international dialogue, regulatory convergence and the ongoing refinement of frameworks and best practices to ensure that AI systems are safe, effective and capable of improving health outcomes across different contexts.

abstract:
The safe transport of infectious substances is a critical component of global health security, requiring rigorous application of international regulations to prevent exposure risks to people and the environment. This guidance document provides a comprehensive and periodically updated framework to support compliance with regulatory requirements applicable as of 1 October 2023, drawing on international, regional and national instruments governing the transport of dangerous goods.

It outlines the processes for identifying, classifying and preparing infectious substances for transport, including distinctions between categories of risk and corresponding packaging, marking, labelling and documentation requirements. The document describes the roles and responsibilities of key stakeholders—such as shippers, carriers, packaging suppliers and receivers—and emphasizes the importance of training and coordination across the transport chain. It also aims to facilitate regulatory harmonization across jurisdictions by reflecting internationally recognized standards and modal agreements. In addition, it examines regulatory variations across transport modes, as well as procedures for managing incidents, ensuring security, and complying with customs and border controls. Intended for professionals involved in shipping infectious materials, this guidance supports the consistent and safe movement of biological substances across borders.

title: Access to medicines
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: Access to medicines is at the core of universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. Despite progress over the past decade in improving access to essential medicines in the Region, this has not been uniform. As health needs in the Region evolve, Member States face increasing challenges in ensuring equitable access to a growing range of quality essential medicines at affordable prices. Access to medicines has been a Flagship Priority for the WHO South-East Asia Region since 2014. An earlier version of the attached working paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. It reviewed the current situation, progress and challenges; outlined some emerging messages and suggested a way forward. The HLP Meeting discussed these, and recommended that the paper should be revised after the Regional Consultation on access to medicines for universal health coverage (16–18 August 2017), so that recommendations from the consultation could be included for consideration by the Seventieth Session of the Regional Committee. The Regional Consultation recommended four areas for inter-country collaboration to advance the medicines agenda. These are: a) information sharing on medicines prices, building on existing platforms; b) information sharing on medicines quality, through the South-East Asia Regulators Network (SEARN); c) taking small but concrete steps in multicounty collaboration on procurement by starting with antidotes (which are lifesaving, and often hard to obtain rapidly); and d) supporting more systematic approaches to bilateral collaboration in procurement. Additional regional actions to strengthen regulatory systems for medical products through SEARN will focus on making greater use by Member States of reliance on each other’s regulatory decisions, to improve regulatory performance. The results of the HLP Meeting deliberations and recommendations from the Regional Consultation are presented below.Actions by Member States (1) Individual country actions, which include: a) Maintain national medicines policies and essential medicines lists as the backbone of action to improve access, supported by sufficient resources for implementation; b) Action to strengthen procurement, pricing and regulation of medical products, and make appropriate use of TRIPS flexibilities; c) Action to encourage more appropriate medicines use, especially of antimicrobials; d) Better monitoring of access to medicines. (2) Greater inter-country cooperation, beginning with four priorities: a) Information sharing on price, building on an existing platform. b) Information sharing on medicines quality, through SEARN. c) Initiate small but concrete collaboration in procurement, starting with antidotes. d) Bilateral cooperation agreements: development of more systematic approaches. Actions by WHO (1) Foster inter-country and regional cooperation in procurement, pricing and regulation of medical products, focused on the four agreed priorities, with short- and medium-term deliverables, (2) Technical support to build capacity as needed, (3) Support improved data on access to and use of medicines, with a focus on antimicrobials. This working paper and the recommendations from the HLP Meeting and the Regional Consultation on access to medicines for universal health coverage are submitted to the Seventieth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration and decision.

Using epilepsy and Parkinson disease as tracer conditions, the report reviews evidence from all WHO regions and explores barriers affecting access across health systems.

Drawing on a landscape analysis and expert consultation, the publication examines key determinants of access, including stigma and awareness, selection and use of essential medicines, regulatory processes, financing, affordability, medicine availability, workforce capacity, health information systems, supply chains, local manufacturing, and pharmacovigilance. title: A controversial change in the sustainable development goal indicator for access to medicines
authors: Joosse, IR; Doblas Rodríguez de Guzmán, L; Mantel-Teeuwisse, AK; Ham, HA van dem
abstract:
This perspective examines the replacement of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 3.b.3, which measures the availability and affordability of essential medicines, with a new health product access index adopted in 2025. The authors argue that the original indicator remains an essential tool for monitoring access to medicines and contend that its limitations, including limited data coverage, complex data collection and methodological challenges, could be addressed through improvements such as electronic data collection, sentinel-site monitoring and simplified analytical approaches rather than by abandoning the indicator altogether.

The article critiques the replacement index for relying primarily on existing health service coverage indicators while failing to adequately measure the availability and affordability of essential medicines, particularly for noncommunicable diseases and children. It also questions the lack of validation of the new index before adoption and its limited usefulness for policy-making. The authors call for continued application of validated methods for monitoring access to essential medicines alongside the new index, while advocating more efficient data collection systems and the development of improved indicators beyond 2030 to support accurate, comprehensive and actionable monitoring of access to medicines worldwide.

title: Access to medicines in countries participating in the WHO Small Countries Initiative: a report on progress, 2024
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: Small countries in the WHO European Region face challenges in access to medicines owing to the small size of their pharmaceutical markets, low negotiating power and country-specific requirements – such as the need to produce tailored health technology assessments (HTAs), pricing and reimbursement dossiers, packaging and leaflets in local languages. These challenges are not new and considered in depth in a policy brief published in 2023 entitled, “Issues and challenges in access to medicines faced by small countries in the WHO European Region”. Proposed mechanisms such as the development of HTAs, managed entry agreements and horizon scanning processes require specialized resources and knowledge, which are often less available in small countries, leading to less favourable procurement terms for public payers. Strengthening and expanding financial protection through voluntary cooperation on joint horizon scanning, pooled demand and procurement, and HTA integration are promising strategies to help countries address these challenges. Areas of particular concern include access to medicines for rare diseases and cancer, and support to ensure that these are available for all patients who need them and affordable by all small countries. title: Issues and challenges in access to medicines faced by small countries in the WHO European Region: policy brief.
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: Essential medicines save lives and improve health when they are available, affordable, of assured quality and properly used. Lack of access to essential medicines is one of the most serious global public health problems and many new medicines are becoming expensive even for the health systems of high- and middle-income countries. This policy brief focuses on the issues and challenges in access to medicines faced by the 11 countries of the WHO Regional Office for Europe Small Countries Initiative. Many of these countries’ challenges arise from or are aggravated because of the size of their pharmaceutical markets. Small countries have low negotiating power and country-specific requirements such as producing tailored health technology assessment (HTA) and pricing and reimbursement dossiers, packaging and leaflets in local languages also decreases the appeal for marketing products in small countries. Furthermore, development of HTA, managed entry agreements and horizon scanning processes requires resources and specialized knowledge and skills often less available in small countries, leading to less favourable procurement terms for public payers. The strategy to address these issues and challenges is through voluntary cooperation, on joint horizon scanning, pooled demand and procurement, and HTA integration, which the Access to Novel Medicines Platform can support.

title: Challenges and opportunities in improving access to medicines through efficient public procurement in the WHO European Region
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: This  report  maps  different  methods  used  by  countries  to  conduct  more  efficient  procurement  and  to  improve  access  to  treatment,  with  a  focus  on  procurement  of  medicines.  Efficient  procurement  involves  more  than  just  obtaining  the  lowest  price – it is about creating a healthy market where high-quality products are available at the right time at affordable prices and at the right quantity. Strategic procurement encompasses all activities aimed at improving procurement efficiency. These include, for example, activities to minimize low-value repetitive purchases, to increase the benefit of economies of scale and to reduce transaction and transport costs. In pharmaceutical procurement additional instruments can be leveraged to improve efficiency:  using  of  generics  or  biosimilar  products;  reducing  the  number  of  medicines  procured  in  a  particular  therapeutic  area, implementation of clinical guidelines and formularies; and creating a competitive market through therapeutic tenders. A country consultation was organized to review national procurement experiences and explore opportunities for collaboration between countries to address key challenges faced in introducing new medicines. It was noted that access to new medicines in Europe could be further facilitated through regional or subregional country collaboration on public procurement of medicines. Discussion points were formulated on how to improve access to new medicines by enhancing the efficiency of procurement systems. A number of initiatives have been set up in recent years. Voluntary collaboration between countries in Europe could also increase efficiency in procurement, and discussion about the possibility of increasing this is growing.

title: Using digital technologies to make access to medicines and dental care more affordable: a case study from Estonia
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This case study examines how Estonia has used digital technologies alongside health coverage reforms to improve affordable access to outpatient prescription medicines and dental care. The publication analyses the development and implementation of digital systems that support financial protection by reducing out-of-pocket payments and simplifying access to benefits. It describes the evolution of Estonia’s health financing and digital health infrastructure, including the national identification system, digital claims management and the national health information system, which enabled automated and real-time administration of health benefits.

The report focuses on two major reforms: the automation of additional medicines benefits through the e-prescription system and the transformation of dental care benefits from retrospective cash reimbursements into in-kind benefits provided at the point of service. It outlines the design of the digital processes, interoperability mechanisms and data exchange systems supporting these reforms, as well as their implementation costs and operational impacts. The study concludes that digital technologies can facilitate coverage expansion, reduce administrative burden and improve access to care, while highlighting remaining challenges related to financial protection, particularly for low-income households and people with high health care needs.

title: Access to affordable medicines for HIV/AIDS and hepatitis
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: This publication was prepared for Twenty-third Meeting of the National AIDS Programme Managers held in New Delhi, India, from 1 to 4 July 2014. The meeting focused on measures needed to further strengthen the health sector response to HIV/AIDS in the South East Asia Region. The successful pursuit of science to win against HIV infection has resulted in a vision of the end of AIDS. As antiretroviral treatment (ART) is scaled up, more people start ART earlier and for prolonged periods of time the consequences of drug resistance to HIV, costly second- and third- line treatments, increased health-care costs, and need for developing newer drugs are important issues. Intellectual property (IP), in particular patents, have been at the centre of the debate on access to affordable medicines for HIV/AIDS. This publication traces IP developments from the inception of the South Africa HIV/AIDS crisis leading to adoption of Doha Declaration for Public Health in WTO in 2001 and the Doha Declaration Para 6 Waiver . The Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Agreement) of the World Trade Organization (WTO) flexibilities including compulsory licensing and voluntary licensing options have been examined. Further, present legal landscape changes and challenges including new research and development models are discussed. A number of options for Member States for promoting access to medicines are described. A number of measures are suggested for achieving the goal of access to affordable medicines for HIV/AIDS and hepatitis and for securing the public health needs for all populations beyond 2015. Access to affordable medicines for HIV/AIDS is linked to intellectual property rights, in particular patents. The lessons from the engagement for generic anti- retroviral drugs holds true for many medical products.

title: Accelerating innovation and access to better medicines for children: advocacy brief
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This advocacy brief addresses persistent inequities in access to safe, effective, quality-assured and age-appropriate medicines for children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Despite major advances in child survival, many essential medicines are unavailable, unsuitable for paediatric use, or introduced years after adult formulations. The document outlines the barriers affecting the development, regulation, production, procurement and delivery of child-friendly medicines, including limited investment in paediatric research and development, fragmented coordination across stakeholders, regulatory challenges, market disincentives, and weaknesses in health system readiness. Framed within the context of global commitments to child health and access to medicines, the brief highlights the consequences of delayed access to optimal treatments for children across multiple disease areas.

Developed by the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations (GAP-f), the publication aims to strengthen advocacy for improved access to better medicines for children. It proposes five priority areas for action: prioritizing key paediatric formulations, strengthening coordination, incentivizing research and market entry, ensuring accessibility and sustainable introduction of medicines at country level, and mobilizing increased and better-targeted investments. The brief calls on governments, international organizations, donors, civil society and other stakeholders to collaborate in advancing policies, financing and implementation strategies that accelerate the availability and uptake of optimal paediatric medicines worldwide.

title: Towards closing the gap in access to child-friendly formulations of essential medicines
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Ensuring equitable access to safe, effective and age-appropriate medicines for children remains a major global public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where suitable paediatric formulations are often unavailable, inadequately adapted or difficult to access. This WHO technical report summarizes a four-year body of work led under the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations (GAP-f) to evaluate the age-appropriateness of medicines included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (EMLc) and identify priority formulation gaps requiring coordinated action.

The publication describes surveys of health-care workers, analyses of market availability and utilization patterns, and a systematic review of medicines and dosage forms using a dedicated paediatric quality product profile assessment tool. The assessment framework examines attributes such as dose flexibility, acceptability, excipient safety, administration requirements, stability, packaging and regulatory status, with particular attention to the realities of resource-constrained settings. The report outlines how the review of hundreds of medicines and formulations informed evidence-based updates to the 2023 and 2025 EMLc, supported paediatric drug optimization exercises and guided the identification of priority formulations for antibiotics, cancer medicines and other therapeutic areas. Intended for regulators, procurement agencies, policy-makers, manufacturers and global health partners, the report also highlights strategic priorities to strengthen research, development, procurement and equitable access to child-friendly essential medicines worldwide.

abstract: This report, with a focus on sustainable access to new medicines, reviews policies that affect medicines throughout their lifecycle (from research and development to disinvestment), examining the current evidence base across Europe. The study features findings from 27 countries and explores different ways that health authorities in European countries are dealing with high spending on new medicines, including methods such as restrictive treatment guidelines, target levels for use of generics, and limitations on the use of particularly expensive drugs. title: Access to essential medicines, vaccines and health technologies: fact sheet on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): health targets
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) aim to transform our world. They are a call to action to end poverty and inequality, protect the planet, and ensure that all people enjoy health, justice and prosperity. It is critical that no one is left behind. In 2015, all the countries in the United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It sets out 17 Goals, which include 169 targets. These wide-ranging and ambitious Goals interconnect. SDG 3 is to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages. It has 13 targets measured through 26 indicators. However, a person’s health and well-being are affected not only by disease and treatment, but also by social and economic factors such as housing, poverty and education. Health targets can therefore also be found across the other SDGs. Vaccines are universally considered to be one of the most successful and cost-effective medical interventions ever introduced. They are a critical tool to reduce health inequality and ensure the greatest possible protection of health and well-being. SDG 3.b urges sustained effort to ensure that everyone has access to the affordable, high-quality medicines and technologies they need. This fact sheet includes facts and figures, outlines the challenges, charts indicators of progress and shares commitments made by Member States to tackle this issue.

title: Efficacy of constitutional support to enhance access to essential medicines as a human right to health in the Eastern Mediterranean Region
authors: Elsayed, L.M.
abstract: Access to essential medicines is an element of the international agreements on the human right to health. This review summarizes the current situation concerning access to medicines in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [EMR] by examining the policies, constitutional provisions and other legal instruments of the Member States. The constitutions of 18 out of 22 EMR countries enshrine health as a human right [8 countries have a duty statement, 5 have a programmatic statement and 5 specify entitlement]; only 4 EMR countries do not enshrine health as a human right in a clause in their constitution. More than half the countries [i.e. 12] have an official national medicines policy, 4 have a draft policy and 6 have no national medicines policy. A total of 11 countries operate an essential medicines list. Realization of this right to health necessitates that duty bearers take all necessary legislative measures to respect, protect and fulfil this right

title: Medicines Transparency Alliance (MeTA): pathways to transparency, accountability an access: cross-case analysis and review of phase II
authors: World Health Organization; Vian, T; Kohler, JC; Dan, L
abstract:
The Medicines Transparency Alliance (MeTA): Pathways to Transparency, Accountability and Access presents a cross-case analysis of Phase II of the MeTA initiative, implemented between 2011 and 2015 in Ghana, Jordan, Kyrgyzstan, Peru, the Philippines, Uganda and Zambia. The review examines how country programmes promoted transparency and accountability in the pharmaceutical sector and explores the relationship between these governance approaches and efforts to improve access to medicines. Using case study methods and archival documentation, the report analyses transparency and accountability mechanisms across participating countries and compares common themes, strategies and experiences.

The analysis found that, although countries rarely adopted explicit definitions or formal models of transparency and accountability, they generally promoted the collection, dissemination and use of information through proactive disclosure, public dialogue and stakeholder engagement. Accountability initiatives centred on multi-stakeholder policy dialogue, strengthening civil society capacity, institutionalizing access to information and citizen education. The report concludes that MeTA generated important outputs in transparency and accountability, while emphasizing that the long-term sustainability of these achievements depends on their institutionalization and the continued participation of governments, civil society and other stakeholders in pharmaceutical governance.

authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
The Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations (GAP-f) is a WHO-hosted network established to address critical gaps in the development, availability and access to age-appropriate medicines for children. This progress report reviews achievements, challenges and lessons learned during the implementation of GAP-f’s 2022–2024 strategic plan. Operating across the full product life cycle, the initiative aims to accelerate the prioritization, evaluation, development, regulatory approval and delivery of paediatric formulations through collaboration among governments, researchers, industry, civil society and international partners. The report describes activities organized under three strategic pillars: prioritizing and aligning global needs, accelerating innovation and access, and intervening to address unmet priorities.

The report highlights progress in identifying formulation priorities across multiple therapeutic areas, strengthening coordination through the paediatric drug optimization process, advancing innovative clinical trial platforms, developing tools to support product introduction, and promoting regulatory alignment and data-sharing initiatives. It also presents examples of work related to HIV, tuberculosis, hepatitis C, childhood cancers, antimicrobial resistance and neglected tropical diseases. The report concludes by outlining priorities for the next strategic phase and emphasizing the importance of sustained collaboration, investment and innovation to improve equitable access to safe, effective and child-friendly medicines worldwide.

title: The selection and use of essential medicines: report of the WHO Expert Committee on Selection and Use of Essential Medicines, 2019 (including the 21st WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and the 7th WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children)
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This report presents the recommendations of the 22nd WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines following its review and update of the 21st WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) and the 7th WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (EMLc). Drawing on systematic evaluation of comparative effectiveness, safety and cost–effectiveness, the Committee assessed applications for new medicines, new formulations, expanded indications and deletions, together with recommendations from the Antibiotics and Cancer Medicines Working Groups. The report summarizes the evidence supporting each decision and the resulting changes to the Model Lists.

The recommendations strengthen the Model Lists across multiple therapeutic areas, with particular emphasis on antimicrobial stewardship through the expansion of the AWaRe classification, improved treatment options for multidrug-resistant infections, tuberculosis, HIV, hepatitis C, malaria and selected noncommunicable diseases, and broader access to essential cancer medicines and reproductive health interventions. The report also addresses challenges related to affordability and access, including insulin and biosimilars, highlights priorities for implementation and future evidence generation, and includes the updated 2019 WHO Model Lists and their classification according to the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical system.

title: The world medicines situation 2011: selection of essential medicines
authors: Ham, Rianne van den; Bero, Lisa; Laing, Richard
abstract:
This publication reviews the evolution, current status and future challenges of the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and its role in improving access to priority medicines through evidence-based selection. It describes the principles underlying the concept of essential medicines, the development of the WHO Model List since 1977, and the transition from expert opinion to a transparent process based on systematic assessment of efficacy, safety, comparative cost-effectiveness and public health relevance. The publication also examines the relationship between national essential medicines lists and standard treatment guidelines, emphasizing their importance for rational medicine selection, procurement and supply within functioning health systems.

The document analyses the adoption and use of national essential medicines lists, the expansion of the Model List to include medicines for children, and variations between WHO and national lists. It discusses emerging challenges in the selection of medicines for children, reproductive health, oncology and orphan diseases, highlighting the need for appropriate evidence, regular updating and country-specific adaptation. The chapter concludes that well-maintained national essential medicines lists, supported by transparent selection procedures and evidence-based treatment guidelines, enable countries to make more effective use of limited resources while improving access to essential medicines for priority health needs.

title: Regional workshop on strengthening quantification and procurement of essential medicines
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: This regional workshop on Strengthening Quantification and Procurement of Medicines was held 10-12 June 2014 to improve efficient medicines procurement and quantification mechanisms and processes. Information was shared on all aspects of drug quantification and procurement. Ten of eleven Member States of the Region participated in the workshop. All countries had conducted a situational analysis of medicines in health care delivery during 2010-2013 and during the workshop each country developed an action plan to strengthen drug supply building on past findings and taking into account technical information and support provided during the workshop. Plenary discussion took place on how countries of the region could work together to support each other in medicines procurement. It was concluded that all countries need to establish unified, wide-reaching electronic drug management information systems for better quantification and medicines management and that availability of essential medicines should be monitored and Standard Operating Procedures followed for all aspects of drug management. It was further concluded that mechanisms need to be established to share information that could ease drug procurement such as drug prices, supplier performance, product quality problems, and registration status of pharmaceutical products.

title: Medicines for treatment of older people in guidelines and essential medicines lists, WHO African Región
authors: Foong, Ke Wei; Paveley, Amelia; Alcock, Isabella; Gorejena-Chidawanyika, Pamela; Gregson, Celia L; Pearson, Grace ME
abstract:
Population ageing is accelerating rapidly in the WHO African Region, creating growing demands on health systems to manage complex, multimorbid conditions among older people. This research article examines the extent to which geriatric medicine is incorporated into national standard treatment guidelines and essential medicines lists across 47 countries, based on a review of national policy documents, with the aim of identifying gaps and opportunities for strengthening clinical guidance and workforce capacity.

The study analyses the presence of dedicated geriatric content and guidance on key conditions, including frailty, dementia, falls, palliative care, osteoporosis, parkinsonism, incontinence, delirium and polypharmacy. Findings indicate that only a small proportion of documents include comprehensive geriatric coverage, with guidance unevenly distributed and often embedded within other specialties. While parkinsonism is widely addressed, critical areas such as frailty and polypharmacy remain largely underrepresented. Inclusion of geriatric guidance is more frequent in countries with higher proportions of older populations and is associated with selected health and demographic indicators. The article highlights structural, educational and resource-related constraints limiting integration of geriatric care, and underscores the need to strengthen national guidelines and medicines lists to inform policy development, training and more person-centred care for ageing populations.

title: Establishing links between drug registers and essential medicines lists
authors: Brhlikova, Petra; Babar, Zaheer-Ud-Din; Pollock, Allyson M
abstract:
Access to essential medicines remains inadequate in many countries despite their central role in universal health coverage and public health policy. This policy and practice article examines the gap between national essential medicines lists and national drug registers, highlighting how the absence of registered products for many essential medicines can limit their availability. Drawing on evidence from several low- and middle-income countries, the authors show that substantial proportions of medicines included on essential medicines lists have no corresponding registered products, while numerous non-essential medicines are authorized for local markets. This misalignment may contribute to inappropriate medicine use, including antimicrobial misuse, and weaken efforts to meet public health priorities.

The article argues for establishing systematic links between national drug registers and essential medicines lists through standardized, digitized data systems. It outlines how shared data variables and routine monitoring could help regulators identify registration gaps, prioritize essential medicines, support rational medicine use and inform policies on procurement, pricing and local production. The authors propose that regulatory authorities give greater priority to medicines included on national essential medicines lists and encourage harmonized data standards to strengthen medicine availability and support more effective health system decision-making.

title: The selection and use of essential medicines 2023: executive summary of the report of the 24th WHO Expert Committee on Selection and Use of Essential Medicines, 24-28 April 2023
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
The selection and use of essential medicines 2023 presents the executive summary of the report of the 24th WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines, convened in Geneva in April 2023 to review and update the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) and the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (EMLc). The document outlines the evidence-based process used to assess applications for the addition, deletion and modification of medicines, indications and formulations, taking into account public health relevance, efficacy, safety, age appropriateness and comparative cost–effectiveness. It also summarizes the Committee’s review of formulations suitable for children and its role in supporting access to essential health products.

The report describes recommendations across a broad range of therapeutic areas, including infectious diseases, noncommunicable diseases, cancer, neurological disorders, tuberculosis, cardiovascular diseases, reproductive health and nutrition. It records decisions on new medicines, therapeutic alternatives, dosage forms and updated indications, as well as proposals that were not recommended. The publication highlights the function of the WHO Model Lists as a reference for countries and regional authorities in developing and revising national essential medicines lists, with the aim of improving access to quality-assured, affordable medicines and promoting their appropriate use within health systems.

title: Parkinson disease treatments on national essential medicines lists, African Region
authors: Fothergill-Misbah, Natasha; Cataldi, Rodrigo; Stothard, Mark; Chowdhary, Neerja; Okubadejo, Njideka; Cappello, Bernadette; Walker, Richard; Dua, Tarun
abstract:
The increasing global burden of Parkinson disease, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, underscores the need to strengthen access to essential medicines and improve health system preparedness. This policy and practice article examines the inclusion of Parkinson disease treatments in national essential medicines lists across 47 countries in the WHO African Region, assessing alignment with the 23rd WHO Model list of essential medicines . It analyses the availability of key therapeutic options, including levodopa combinations and anticholinergic medicines, and explores how inclusion patterns relate to broader access challenges.

The analysis shows that 81% of countries include levodopa combined with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor and 79% include an anticholinergic alternative, although only a minority include recommended formulations such as the 4:1 ratio, and 11% include none of the key medicines. It highlights multiple structural barriers affecting access, including limited prioritization of Parkinson disease, shortages of trained health personnel, regulatory and financing constraints, and gaps in data on disease burden. While inclusion in national essential medicines lists does not ensure availability, it can support procurement, prescribing and policy prioritization. The study underscores the importance of regularly updating these lists in line with WHO guidance and local epidemiology, alongside strengthening regulatory systems, workforce capacity and supply mechanisms to improve equitable access to treatment.

title: Prices, availability and affordability of selected essential medicines for chronic diseases in Türkiye
authors: Gökçen Özler; Oguz Isik
abstract: Background:Fair access to essential medicines is a significant parameter in fulfilling the right to basic health.Aim:We investigated the availability, prices and affordability of essential medicines for chronic diseases in Ankara, Türkiye.Methods:We used the procedures outlined in the WHO and Health Action International guidelines for measuring prices, availability, affordability, and price components of medicines. The sample consisted of 334 (14%) of the 2354 pharmacies in Ankara, and 24 essential medicines for cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, chronic respiratory diseases, and palliative care, adopted from the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2021). We collected the data in 2021 using a questionnaire administered through face-to-face survey and analysed the data using SPSS version 22.Results:The findings showed that 15 medicines (62.5% of the selected medicines) met the 80% availability target set by WHO, while 9 did not. The original medicines were more readily available than the generic ones. Among the original medicines, furosemide (10.11) and acetylsalicylic acid (9.26) had the highest median price ratios. The generic medicines seemed to be more affordable than original medicines. Glibenclamide, budesonide, gliclazide, and diazepam had low availability and were sold at higher prices than their international reference prices.Conclusion:This research highlights priority areas of action to improve access to affordable medicines for chronic diseases in Ankara, Türkiye.

title: Executive summary: the selection and use of essential medicines 2019: report of the 22nd WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines: WHO Headquarters, Geneva, 1-5 April 2019
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This executive summary presents the recommendations of the 22nd WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines following its review of applications to update the 2019 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) and the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (EMLc). Based on systematic assessment of comparative effectiveness, safety and cost–effectiveness, the Committee evaluated proposals for new medicines, new formulations, expanded indications and deletions, as well as recommendations from the Antibiotics and Cancer Medicines Working Groups. The report summarizes the evidence underpinning additions, modifications and removals across a broad range of therapeutic areas and highlights major revisions to the structure and content of the Model Lists.

Particular emphasis is placed on strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through the integration and expansion of the AWaRe classification of antibiotics, improving access to effective treatments for priority infectious diseases, cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and reproductive health, and aligning the Model Lists with current WHO guidelines. The report also addresses broader policy issues affecting access to essential medicines, including affordability, biosimilars, procurement strategies, intellectual property, and the role of the Medicines Patent Pool. It identifies priorities for future evidence generation and recommends continued work to support implementation of the Model Lists and equitable access to essential medicines worldwide.

title: Improving national alignment to mark 50 years of WHO’s essential medicines lists
authors: Moja, Lorenzo; Cappello, Bernadette; Mubangizi, Deusdedit
abstract:
Ensuring equitable access to essential medicines remains a cornerstone of effective health systems, requiring policies that prioritize population needs and rational resource use. This editorial examines the evolution and continued relevance of the World Health Organization’s model list of essential medicines, originally developed to guide medicine selection based on public health priorities rather than market forces, and its role in shaping national selection, procurement and access strategies over the past five decades.

The article describes how the model list has adapted to changing disease patterns and therapeutic advances while maintaining a focus on clinical value, safety and public health impact. It identifies persistent challenges in aligning national essential medicines lists with global standards, including outdated selection practices, insufficient specification of formulations and indications, and fragmentation in procurement processes. These limitations can hinder accurate forecasting, weaken supply chains and increase the risk of medicine shortages. The discussion emphasizes the importance of transparent governance, regular updates and context-specific prioritization to strengthen national lists as effective policy and operational tools for planning and procurement. The editorial calls for renewed accountability and coordinated action among policy-makers, encouraging countries to use the fiftieth anniversary of the model list as an opportunity to improve alignment, support sustainable financing and enhance access to quality-assured medicines across diverse settings.

authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: Access to affordable quality-assured essential medicines and vaccines has been recognized as a crucial element of the solutions to numerous important public health problems in World Health Assembly resolutions. It also represents one of the targets of the Sustainable Development Goals and is essential to achieving universal health coverage.Unfortunately, availability is not always guaranteed, and more and more countries are facing shortages of essential medicines and vaccines. In order to gain a better, more comprehensive understanding of the national mechanisms in place and of strategies used by countries to mitigate the risk of shortages, WHO developed a survey to assess the extent and impact of shortages across countries and sent it to all Member States in the WHO European Region in 2018. This report summarizes the main findings and considerations arising from the responses.

title: Instructions for applicants preparing a submission for the 2025 meeting of the WHO Expert Committee on Selection and Use of Essential Medicines
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This document provides mandatory instructions for preparing submissions to the 2025 meeting of the WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines for proposals to include new medicines or new indications for medicines already listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) and the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (EMLc). It defines the required submission format, minimum evidence standards and documentation necessary for proposals to be considered by the Expert Committee, and outlines the submission process, timelines and consultation requirements with WHO technical departments and other stakeholders.
The guidance describes the information to be included in each section of a submission, covering the public health relevance of the proposed medicine, treatment details, evidence on comparative benefits and harms, recommendations in current clinical guidelines, comparative costs and cost–effectiveness, regulatory status, market availability and pharmacopoeial standards. It also specifies methodological expectations for systematic literature searches, evidence synthesis, use of GRADE assessments, and transparent reporting of references. The document aims to promote consistency, transparency and evidence-based evaluation in the review of applications for inclusion or modification of medicines on the WHO Model Lists.

title: Revising the procedures for updating WHO’s Model Lists of Essential Medicines: consultation report, Geneva, Switzerland, 2-3 November 2023
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This consultation report summarizes discussions held at WHO headquarters in Geneva in November 2023 on revising the procedures for updating the WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines (EML and EMLc). The meeting brought together international experts and stakeholders to examine whether the current selection process, established in 2001, remains fit for purpose in the context of evolving medical innovation, increasingly complex health technologies, and persistent barriers to equitable access to essential medicines. The report reviews the role of the EML in supporting universal health coverage and highlights challenges related to medicine affordability, feasibility of implementation, evidence assessment, and access in different health system settings.

The document presents key themes and strategic directions identified during the consultation. These include strengthening alignment between the EML and WHO guidelines, improving transparency and dissemination of decisions, learning from rejected applications, enhancing the use of information on price, cost and cost-effectiveness, and promoting policies that improve access to essential medicines. It also explores considerations for medicine selection during public health emergencies and discusses opportunities to modernize EML processes through digital tools, improved evidence synthesis, stronger partnerships, and enhanced monitoring of real-world implementation. The report is intended to inform future revisions of WHO procedures for updating the Model Lists of Essential Medicines.

authors: Meenakshi V Chivukula; Klara Tisocki
abstract: Background In 2015, the need for equitable access to cancer treatments in low- and middle incomecountries was underscored by the addition of 16 essential cancer medicines to the 19th World HealthOrganization (WHO) model list of essential medicines (WHO EML). This study assessed the degree towhich this expanded WHO EML from 2015 has influenced inclusion of cancer medicines in the mostrecent national essential medicines lists of the countries of the WHO South-East Asia Region.Methods The inclusion of a selected list of 38 essential cancer medicines in the 2015 WHO EML wasassessed in the most recent national lists of essential medicines from the 11 countries of the WHOSouth-East Asia Region. Additionally, the availability of six essential cancer medicines common tothe national lists of essential medicines from six countries of the WHO South-East Asia Region wasexplored.Results Of the 38 selected essential cancer medicines included in the 19th WHO EML, a mean of 18.0(range 2–33) were included in the national lists of countries of the WHO South-East Asia Region. Ofthe 25 essential cancer medicines included in the WHO EML prior to the 19th revision, a mean of 14.6(range 2–21) were included in national lists; notably fewer of the 13 cancer medicines added in the2015 revision were included: mean 3.4 (range 0–12).Conclusion Compared with the WHO EML, there is a lag in the inclusion of essential cancermedicines in national lists of essential medicines in the WHO South-East Asia Region. Alignment ofessential cancer medicines in national lists of essential medicines among the 11 countries in the regionvaries significantly. These differences may hinder regional strategies to improve access to essentialcancer medicines, such as pooled procurement of selected high-cost medicines. The link between theavailability and affordability of essential cancer medicines warrants further investigation, in the contextof access to medicines for universal health coverage

title: A cross-sectional survey of the models in Bihar and Tamil Nadu, India for pooled procurement of medicines
authors: Maulik Chokshi; Habib Hasan Farooqui; Sakthivel Selvaraj; Preeti Kumar
abstract: Background: In India, access to medicine in the public sector is significantlyaffected by the efficiency of the drug procurement system and allied processesand policies. This study was conducted in two socioeconomically different states:Bihar and Tamil Nadu. Both have a pooled procurement system for drugs butfollow different models. In Bihar, the volumes of medicines required are pooledat the state level and rate contracted (an open tender process invites biddersto quote for the lowest rate for the list of medicines), while actual invoicing andpayment are done at district level. In Tamil Nadu, medicine quantities are alsopooled at state level but payments are also processed at state level upon receiptof laboratory quality-assurance reports on the medicines.Methods: In this cross-sectional survey, a range of financial and non-financial datarelated to procurement and distribution of medicine, such as budget documents,annual reports, tender documents, details of orders issued, passbook details andpolicy and guidelines for procurement were analysed. In addition, a so-called ABCanalysis of the procurement data was done to to identify high-value medicines.Results: It was observed that Tamil Nadu had suppliers for 100% of the drugson their procurement list at the end of the procurement processes in 2006, 2007and 2008, whereas Bihar’s procurement agency was only able to get suppliersfor 56%, 59% and 38% of drugs during the same period. Further, it was observedthat Bihar’s system was fuelling irrational procurement; for example, fluconazole(antifungal) alone was consuming 23.4% of the state’s drug budget and was beingprocured by around 34% of the districts during 2008–2009. Also, the ratios ofprocurement prices for Bihar compared with Tamil Nadu were in the range of 1.01to 22.50. For 50% of the analysed drugs, the price ratio was more than 2, that is,Bihar’s procurement system was procuring the same medicines at more than twicethe prices paid by Tamil Nadu.Conclusion: Centralized, automated pooled procurement models like that ofTamil Nadu are key to achieving the best procurement prices and highest possibleaccess to medicines

title: WHO procurement report 2023
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Global health programmes and emergency responses rely on robust procurement systems to ensure the timely acquisition and delivery of essential goods and services. This report presents an overview of procurement activities undertaken by the World Health Organization in 2023, within the context of sustained post-pandemic operational demands and institutional commitments to transparency and accountability.

It describes procurement governance, guiding principles and organizational arrangements, and provides detailed statistical analyses of procurement volume, value distribution, categories, suppliers and regional patterns. The document highlights a continued decline in overall procurement following the COVID-19 peak, while remaining above pre-pandemic levels, alongside a predominance of service-related procurement and a concentration of expenditure in higher-value contracts. It also examines procurement mechanisms such as catalogue-based purchasing, regional and collaborative procurement within the United Nations system, and outlines key operational initiatives including supply chain digitalization, long-term agreements for essential medicines, and expanded logistics support to country offices. By situating procurement within the broader delivery of WHO programmes, the report supports informed oversight of procurement practices and their contribution to effective and timely public health interventions.

title: Global market landscape of vaccine manufacturing and procurement
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Global disparities in vaccine manufacturing capacity and procurement patterns continue to shape equitable access to immunization and preparedness for future health emergencies. This WHO analytical report examines the current global landscape of vaccine production and procurement using data from 204 countries and 98 manufacturers across multiple production stages, including drug substance production, formulation, filling and packaging. The publication analyses regional procurement trends, manufacturing interdependencies, technology platforms and supplier concentration, while assessing how these factors influence vaccine security, market resilience and pandemic preparedness. It also aims to support strategic decision-making by governments, manufacturers and international organizations involved in vaccine policy, procurement and regional manufacturing initiatives.

The report identifies substantial regional variation in manufacturing capacity and self-reliance, with many low- and middle-income countries remaining dependent on external suppliers and pooled procurement mechanisms. It highlights the concentration of production among a limited number of manufacturers and the dominance of traditional vaccine technologies, while noting that innovative platforms such as mRNA remain concentrated in Europe and the United States. Through regional comparisons and vaccine-specific case studies, the analysis examines vulnerabilities related to supply disruptions, raw material dependencies and limited diversification of suppliers, emphasizing that domestic or regional production alone does not guarantee supply security during health emergencies. The publication also discusses strategic considerations for expanding sustainable regional manufacturing ecosystems, including investments in research and development, regulatory strengthening, workforce capacity and regional coordination mechanisms to improve equitable vaccine access worldwide.

title: Controlling medicine prices in Sudan: the challenge of the recently established Medicines Regulatory Authority
authors: Ali , G.K.M.; Yahia, A.Y.
abstract: This study evaluated the capacity of the medicine pricing mechanism of the National Medicines and Poisons Board [NMPB], the medicine regulatory agency of Sudan, in controlling prices of imported medicines. The study was conducted between July and September 2008 and data on the 50 most sold medicines in 2007 were obtained from the records of the regulatory authority and pharmacies in Khartoum; 135 products were included. The cost and freight [CandF] prices of 23% of the selected medicines approved by NMPB were over 10 times the International Reference Price; 71% of these items were generics. The wholesale price of only 40% of the studied medicines was less than that approved by NMPB, while the retail price of 47% of medicines was less than that approved by the authority. The retail price of 11 of 12 originator medicines was equal to or more than their prices published in the British National Formulary. The price of the medicines distributed by Central Medical Supplies was about 2-fold their C and F price. The current pricing system is of limited benefit in controlling medicine prices in Sudan

title: Medicines reimbursement policies in Europe
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: This report reviews and analyses different reimbursement policies for medicines applied by countries in the WHO European region. The  study  used  a  mixed  methods  approach  including  primary  data  collection  through  a  questionnaire  addressing  the  competent  authorities  included  in  the  Pharmaceutical  Pricing  and  Reimbursement  Information  (PPRI)  network,  a  literature  review,  qualitative  interviews  with  authorities  and  researchers  in  selected  case  study  countries,  and  a  cross-country  analysis  of  the  actual  financial  burden  for  patients.  The  study  found  that  while  almost  all  countries  provide  full  coverage  for  medicines  in  the  inpatient  sector,  patients can be asked to co-pay for reimbursable medicines in the outpatient sector. As a commonly applied co-payment patients pay a defined share of the price of a medicine; in addition, prescription fees and/or deductibles are also in place in some countries. In the countries of the WHO European region, mechanisms have been established to protect defined population groups from excessive co-payments for medicines; key reasons for reductions of and exemptions from co-payments include low income, defined diseases or disabilities and age. The analysis of the actual financial burden suggested that co-payments may pose a substantial financial burden for patients, particularly in lower-income countries. The report identified several principles aiming to improve affordable access to medicines and protect people from excessive out-of-pocket co-payments. These include clear priority-setting processes, evidence-based decision-making, transparent processes, consideration of vulnerable population groups, making use of the efficiency of lower-priced medicines, regular evaluations and strategic design of policy measures.

title: The role of ethics in the rational use of medicine
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: The Constitution of the World Health Organization states that, "The enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being.." Access to essential medicines and their rational use are crucial elements in the delivery of health services and health care and can be seen as a part of the fundamental right to health. This publication highlights the need to observe ethics and codes of conduct by four entitles associated with medicines. The researcher who is concerned with the development and discovery of drugs; the pharmaceutical manufacturer who is involved in the development, production and promotion of the medicines; the medical and allied professionals who prescribe, and dispense them and the government who is responsible for other regulatory control of medicines. Strategies to improve the use of medicines have also been delineated. The are: (1) institution of regulations based on ethics, equity and transparency; (2) research based on Good Clinical Practice; (3) drug development based on needs of countries including orphan drugs, antimalarials and anti-tuberculosis medicines; (4) marketing to be coupled with post-marketing surveillance for regulation of medicines and (5) ethical principles observed by all stakeholders in the medicines chain which includes research and development, clinical trials, registration, manufacturing, patents, prices, distribution, donations and promotion. Ethics should form an indispensable component of the strategy for promoting the rational use of medicines.
