title: Medicine availability and affordability for paediatric cancers, China
authors: Bai, Lin; Huang, Tao; Li, Huangqianyu; Shi, Luwen; Denburg, Avram; Gupta, Sumit; Guan, Xiaodong
abstract:
This study assesses the availability and affordability of essential anticancer medicines for children in China using 2021 drug utilization data from 55 tertiary children’s hospitals across seven geographical regions. The analysis covered all 33 anticancer medicines included in the 2021 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children and evaluated access by examining medicine availability in hospitals and treatment affordability relative to regional disposable income. The study was undertaken in the context of increasing childhood cancer incidence, persistent disparities in survival outcomes and the importance of equitable access to effective pharmacotherapy for improving cancer care.

The findings indicate that access to essential paediatric anticancer medicines remains suboptimal and unevenly distributed across China. Although all medicines studied had received regulatory approval, many were available in fewer than half of surveyed hospitals, and several products imposed substantial financial burdens on families. Medicines approved for paediatric indications showed higher availability than those without such approval, while access to targeted therapies was generally lower than to cytotoxic medicines. Regional differences in availability and affordability were associated with variations in economic development and health-care resources. The study highlights the need for measures to address medicine shortages, strengthen access to essential paediatric cancer treatments and reduce financial barriers to care.

title: A case study on the ecosystem for local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologicals: the Serbia context
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This case study analyses the Serbian ecosystem for local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologicals, with a particular focus on technology transfer and manufacturing capacity for messenger RNA (mRNA) COVID-19 vaccines. Developed within the WHO initiative on strengthening local production, the report examines the national policy, regulatory, financial and research environment relevant to vaccine and biologics production. It reviews Serbia’s legal and institutional frameworks, financing mechanisms, fiscal incentives for research and development, intellectual property protection, regulatory oversight and market conditions, as well as the role of academia, innovation centres and public institutions in supporting technology transfer and local manufacturing.

The publication highlights the historical and current role of the Torlak Institute for Virology, Vaccines and Sera in vaccine production and its participation in the WHO mRNA Technology Transfer Programme. It discusses Serbia’s capacities and challenges related to research infrastructure, workforce development, Good Manufacturing Practice standards, clinical research and regulatory maturity. The report also addresses existing gaps, including limited dedicated incentives for local mRNA vaccine production and the need for further technological preparedness and investment, while outlining ongoing initiatives and recommendations to strengthen sustainable local production and health security.

title: A case study on the ecosystem for local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologicals: the Bangladesh context
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This case study examines the ecosystem for local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologicals in Bangladesh, with particular attention to the development of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines. Based on literature reviews, stakeholder consultations, interviews and policy analysis conducted in 2022, the report assesses the country’s policy environment, financing mechanisms, regulatory systems, research and development capacity, intellectual property framework, technology transfer opportunities and manufacturing preparedness. It explores the role of government institutions, regulatory authorities and private-sector actors in supporting vaccine access and strengthening local production capabilities within the broader context of universal health coverage and global health security.

The publication reviews Bangladesh’s evolving vaccine ecosystem, including the introduction of mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, current manufacturing activities, regulatory pathways and capacity-building initiatives. It identifies challenges related to research infrastructure, regulatory maturity, market conditions, technology transfer and financing, while outlining strategies to support sustainable local production of vaccines and biologicals. The report also highlights the achievements of Bangladesh’s pharmaceutical sector, which supplies most domestic medicine needs and exports products internationally, while noting continued dependence on imports for vaccines and certain biological products. The findings provide an overview of opportunities and constraints affecting the country’s efforts to expand local production and strengthen access to quality-assured health products.

Nigeria remains heavily dependent on imported vaccines and a large proportion of its pharmaceutical products despite having a sizeable and growing pharmaceutical manufacturing industry. This case study examines the ecosystem for local production of pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologicals in Nigeria, with particular attention to preparedness for vaccine manufacturing and participation in the WHO mRNA technology transfer initiative. The publication also reviews national strategies and partner-supported initiatives aimed at strengthening local production and re-establishing vaccine manufacturing capacity. It concludes with recommendations to enhance coordination, investment, regulatory capacity and innovation in support of sustainable local production, improved access to quality-assured health products and greater health security in Nigeria.

title: Artificial intelligence applied to local production of diagnostic tests
authors: Dong, Jicui; Woo, David; Kostaridou, Vasileia; Wang, Yan; Resende, Virginia Maria Ferreira
abstract:
Strengthening local production of in vitro diagnostic medical devices is essential to improve access to timely, affordable and quality-assured diagnostics, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where health systems face structural constraints, and especially during health emergencies and pandemics. This perspective article examines the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing local production of diagnostic tests, analysing its applications across the value chain and lifecycle of in vitro diagnostics.

The article describes how AI technologies, including machine learning, generative models, digital twins and robotics, can support research and development, product design, manufacturing processes, quality control, supply chain management and regulatory compliance. It highlights opportunities for improving efficiency, reducing costs, strengthening data integration and enabling real-time monitoring, while also identifying key barriers to adoption, such as limited technical capacity, high investment requirements, fragmented regulatory frameworks and challenges related to data quality and interoperability. Ethical considerations, including data privacy, transparency, bias and the need for human oversight, are also examined. The discussion emphasizes the importance of coordinated policy support, capacity-building and international collaboration to enable responsible AI integration, reducing reliance on imports and strengthening production autonomy. Intended for policy-makers, manufacturers and global health stakeholders, it outlines pathways to leverage AI for more resilient and equitable diagnostic production systems.

Based on responses collected through a multilingual survey distributed in 2023, the report analyses how Member States are developing or implementing systems intended to strengthen supply chain integrity, improve oversight and reduce the risks associated with substandard and falsified medical products.

The document identifies varying levels of implementation, ranging from fully operational systems to countries in early planning stages. It highlights key challenges including limited funding, technological constraints, insufficient technical expertise, regulatory gaps and interoperability issues. The publication also reviews the use of global and domestic standards, data carriers such as 2D data matrix technologies, and approaches to data ownership and governance. The findings emphasize the importance of collaboration, knowledge sharing and capacity-building to support the development of effective traceability systems and enhance the security and efficiency of medical product supply chains globally.

title: Availability, pricing and affordability of selected medicines for noncommunicable diseases
authors: Elham Heidari; Mehdi Varmaghani; Akbar Abdollahiasl
abstract:
Background:
The global and national burden of noncommunicable diseases continues to rise, thus making access to medicines increasingly important.
Aims:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the availability, pricing, and affordability of selected medicines for noncommunicable diseases in the Islamic Republic of Iran used in 2014 based on the World Health Organization (WHO)/Health Action International (HAI)methodology.
Methods:
The price and availability data for 54 selected medicines were collected from public and private retail pharmacies as well as private pharmacies located in public hospitals in six cities of the Islamic Republic of Iran on the basis of the standardized methodology developed by WHO and HAI. The outcome measures were percentage availability of medicines, ratios of medicine prices to the international reference prices, and the affordability. Affordability was defined as the number of days’ wages needed by the lowest-paid unskilled government worker to afford one month of chronic treatment.
Results:
The procurement price of the surveyed Lowest Priced Generic and Most Sold Generic medicines was 1.19 times the international reference price. The patient price was not significantly different among different pharmacy retail settings compared with the international reference prices. Moreover, the overall mean availability of the surveyed Lowest Priced Generic medicines in public, private, and other settings was 75.5%, 83.3% and 80.3%, respectively. All the treatment costs for the high burden noncommunicable diseases were less than one day’s wages of the lowest-paid government worker.
Conclusions:
This study indicated that procurement prices of the surveyed medicines were reasonable in comparison with the international reference price. Moreover, the availability of generic forms of the surveyed medicines was good but originator brand medicines were significantly low in all the three settings

title: Price, availability and affordability: an international comparison of chronic disease medicines
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean
abstract: Chronic diseases are a serious public health issue, particularly because they require long-term therapy. Ensuring access to medicines for treating chronic disease, however, remains neglected. In May 2001, the World Health Assembly adopted a resolution stating that WHO should explore systems for monitoring medicine prices with a view to improving access to essential drugs. WHO and Health Action International, in collaboration with a panel of experts, developed a methodology for surveying the prices, availability, affordability and components of medicine prices in developing and transitional countries. This report presents the synthesis data of 14 chronic disease medicines collected in 30 surveys that were undertaken using this methodology between 2001 and 2005. The key recommendation of this report is that to improve access to medicines for chronic diseases, governments should measure and continuously monitor the prices, availability and affordability of medicines and price components. title: Pricing policies for generic medicines in Australia, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea and Singapore: patent expiry and influence on atorvastatin price
authors: Elizabeth E Roughead; Dong-Sook Kim; Benjamin Ong; Anna Kemp-Casey
abstract: Background Little is known about how the different policies available to promote use of genericmedicines affect the price per unit supplied or sold. This study compares the influence of pricingpolicies for generic medicines on atorvastatin prices in Australia, New Zealand, the Republic of Koreaand Singapore, after market entry of generic atorvastatin.Methods The annual price of atorvastatin per defined daily dose supplied (price/DDD) was examinedfor each country from 2006 to 2015 (≥2 years before and ≥4 years after generic market entry). Priceswere converted to international dollars and cumulative percentage price reductions were calculated forthe first 4 years following generic entry.Results Prior to market entry of generic atorvastatin, New Zealand had the lowest price ($0.10/DDD),and the Republic of Korea the highest ($2.89/DDD). The price/DDD fell immediately after generic entryin all countries except New Zealand, which already had low prices. The largest immediate decreasewas observed in Singapore (46%, year 1). By the fourth year after generic entry, the price had fallen by46–80% in all countries; however, large price differences between countries remained.Conclusion New Zealand’s tendering system and use of preferred medicines resulted in verylow atorvastatin prices well before patent expiry. Pricing policies in the other three countries wereeffective in reducing atorvastatin prices, with reductions of between 46% and 80% within 4 years ofgeneric entry. Where tendering and use of preferred medicines were the mechanisms for atorvastatinprocurement (New Zealand), prices were lowest before and after generic entry. Mandatory pricecuts, combined with price-disclosure policies (Australia), produced similar relative price reductions totendering systems (New Zealand, Singapore) at 4 years. By comparison, mandatory price cuts upongeneric entry as the sole measure, while initially effective, were associated with the smallest relativereduction in price after 4 years (Republic of Korea).

This report summarizes the proceedings of a meeting of the World Health Organization Technical Advisory Group on Pricing Policies for Medicines (TAG-PPM), held on 19 November 2025. As an advisory body, the TAG-PPM supports WHO in advancing policies to improve equitable and affordable access to medicines. The meeting aimed to review the group’s work programme, assess progress and define priorities for 2026, within the broader context of strengthening pricing policies, market transparency and evidence-informed decision-making for health products.

The document presents the outcomes of two main workstreams. The first focuses on the development of a standardized framework for economic evidence to inform decisions on medicine listing in normative guidance, including the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. The second examines the economic, social and policy implications of non-transparent medicine pricing and explores strategies to enhance price transparency across the value chain. The report highlights key challenges, including variability in data quality, methodological inconsistencies and limited transparency, and outlines priority areas for further work. Intended for policy-makers, technical experts and stakeholders involved in pharmaceutical policy, it provides a basis for future technical outputs, including technical reports and peer-reviewed publications, and supports ongoing efforts to strengthen access to affordable medicines.

title: WHO guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This second edition WHO guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations to support countries in formulating and implementing pharmaceutical pricing policies that improve affordable and equitable access to quality-assured medicines and vaccines while promoting value for money and maintaining reliable supply. Replacing the 2015 guideline, it reflects updated evidence, accumulated country experience and the growing global concern over unaffordable prices that impede progress towards universal health coverage. Developed according to the WHO handbook for guideline development, the recommendations are based on systematic reviews, GRADE assessment and consideration of implementation, equity, feasibility and sustainability.

The guideline presents eight overarching principles for pharmaceutical pricing policies together with recommendations on ten policy options: external and internal reference pricing, value-based pricing, regulation of supply-chain mark-ups, price transparency, tendering and negotiation, promotion of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines, pooled procurement, cost-plus pricing, and tax exemptions or reductions. It emphasizes that pricing policies should be selected and adapted according to national health system objectives and contexts, implemented alongside complementary measures, and supported by transparent governance, monitoring and regular review. The guideline is intended primarily for policy-makers and decision-makers, while also informing managers responsible for procurement, distribution and reimbursement of pharmaceutical products.

title: Availability, price and affordability of health technologies for the management of diabetes
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This report examines the availability, price and affordability of key health technologies for the management of diabetes, with a focus on blood glucose meters, test strips, lancets, insulin syringes, blood pressure measurement devices and glycated haemoglobin testing. It is produced as part of a WHO initiative under the Global Diabetes Compact to improve access to essential diagnostics and related technologies, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The analysis is based on a scoping review of the literature, compilation of existing price data, and an online survey of biomedical engineers and key opinion leaders.

The findings highlight substantial gaps in the availability of essential medical devices and considerable variability in prices across countries and products. Evidence indicates that the cost of consumables, especially test strips, often exceeds that of the devices themselves and represents a major barrier to sustained self-monitoring. Affordability remains a critical challenge, particularly for glycated haemoglobin testing and routine glucose monitoring. The report underscores the need for improved price transparency, stronger procurement and supply mechanisms, and integration of medical devices into universal health coverage frameworks to enhance equitable access to diabetes care.

title: Pharmaceutical pricing and reimbursement systems in eastern Europe and central Asia: report of the Pharmaceutical Pricing and Reimbursement Information network for countries in eastern Europe and central Asia
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: This report presents pharmaceutical policies related to pricing, purchasing and funding of medicines in 11 countries in eastern Europe and central Asia (Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, the Republic of Moldova, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan). These are among the members of a regional subgroup of the Pharmaceutical Pricing and Reimbursement Information (PPRI) network of competent authorities in the field of pharmaceutical pricing and reimbursement. They mainly provided evidence in the form of national profiles and posters, including information on access to HIV, hepatitis and tuberculosis medicines. The survey showed that seven countries have a form of price regulation in place for all or a limited number of outpatient medicines. Five of these have regulation at all price levels (with policies on the application of external price referencing mark-ups at the wholesale and pharmacy levels). In the hospital sector, medicines are mainly procured through tendering (predominantly via central procurement) and are provided free of charge to patients. Medicines included in national government disease programmes (such as those for HIV and tuberculosis) are also provided free of charge. Other outpatient medicines are purchased by the patient either fully out of pocket or against a co-payment where medicines are part of a benefit package (reimbursement list). This report highlights limitations in equitable access to affordable medicines caused by, among others, high and increasing out-of-pocket payments for outpatient medicines.

title: South Africa’s single exit price 2004-2023

This policy report describes the development, implementation and reported outcomes of South Africa’s Single Exit Price (SEP) system for medicines between 2004 and 2023. Produced as part of the WHO Pharmaceutical Pricing Policy Report Series, the publication examines the introduction of a transparent and standardized medicine pricing mechanism for the private sector, alongside complementary measures such as mandatory generic substitution and regulated dispensing fees. The report outlines the historical context of pharmaceutical price regulation in South Africa following the end of apartheid, including reforms introduced through the National Drug Policy and amendments to the Medicines and Related Substances Act aimed at improving access to medicines and reducing inequities in the health system.

The report reviews governance arrangements, annual price adjustment mechanisms and the role of the pricing committee in administering the policy. It summarizes reported impacts on medicine pricing, affordability and transparency, including reductions in prices for originator and generic medicines and estimated savings within the private health sector. The publication also discusses implementation challenges, including litigation, concerns regarding inflation adjustments and ongoing variability in logistics fees. In addition, it examines issues related to medicine availability, supply chain transparency and the broader relevance of SEP within South Africa’s evolving national health insurance and pharmaceutical policy landscape.

abstract:
This technical report presents the systematic reviews commissioned to update the second edition of the WHO guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies. It synthesizes the evidence on the effects of ten pharmaceutical pricing policies implemented individually or in combination to improve the affordability and availability of medicines for patients and health systems. Developed in response to the expansion of the evidence base since the 2015 WHO guideline, the report assesses the impact of these policies on medicine prices, utilization, availability and affordability, while also examining contextual and implementation factors relevant to policy decisions. The report describes the review methodology, including literature searches, study selection, risk of bias assessment, evidence synthesis and GRADE evidence profiling.

The systematic reviews examine pooled procurement, value-based pricing, discounts for single-source pharmaceuticals, cost-plus pricing, tax exemptions or reductions, promotion of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines, reference pricing, price transparency, regulation of mark-ups across the pharmaceutical supply and distribution chain, and tendering and negotiation. For each policy, the report summarizes the available evidence, evaluates its completeness and quality, identifies implications for policy and practice, and highlights priorities for future research. It provides the evidence base underpinning the updated WHO guideline and supports transparent, evidence-informed pharmaceutical pricing policy development.

title: Towards a new vision for shared responsibility in pharmaceutical pricing, coverage and reimbursement: policy approaches building on principles of solidarity, transparency and sustainability
authors: Docteur, Elizabeth
abstract: Concerns about affordable access to medicines reflect the emergence of new, high-priced medicines, as well as expectations regarding the cost of precision therapies coming to market. Compared with a decade ago, novel medicines are subject to longer delays between global launch and market access, even in wealthier countries. Various paths forward offer potential policy solutions to address problems with access to high-priced pharmaceuticals. This technical report considers four categories of policies – demand pooling, formal tiered pricing, risk-sharing agreements and policies to harness competition – with potential to ameliorate issues in ensuring timely, affordable and equitable access to effective medicines in the WHO European Region. Each approach offers the potential to address a different dimension of the affordability problem. The most promising strategies to tackle affordability of high-priced medicines are likely to entail a combination approach – for example, a test pilot of a single-buyer agreement using a combination of managed-entry agreements and tiered pricing for agreement signatories under an agreed formula. To facilitate policy development, stakeholder commitment to three underlying principles – solidarity, transparency and sustainability – is essential.

title: Protocol deviations in medicine quality tests
authors: Mulatsari, Esti; Saputro, Ismail Dwi; Simanjuntak, Ronal; Ginanjar, Vicky Achmad; Rahmawati, Ayu; Pisannic, Elizabeth; Anggrianic, Yusi
abstract:
Ensuring the quality of medicines is essential for patient safety and for preventing adverse public health outcomes, particularly in settings where substandard and falsified products are prevalent. This policy and practice article examines the challenges of applying pharmacopoeial testing standards in resource-constrained environments, focusing on how deviations from validated protocols can affect the accuracy of medicine quality assessments and potentially lead to misguided policy decisions.

The article describes how national, regional and international pharmacopoeias establish standards and testing methods primarily designed for manufacturing and regulatory contexts, often requiring sophisticated equipment, materials and technical expertise. It analyses the practical constraints faced by researchers and regulators conducting post-marketing surveillance and field surveys, including limited access to monographs, reference standards, equipment and validation capacity. Drawing on a case study of amoxicillin tablet testing in Indonesia, it demonstrates how methodological adaptations, such as modifications in sample preparation, can substantially distort results and lead to misleading estimates of substandard medicines. The discussion also highlights inconsistencies across pharmacopoeias, gaps in transparency regarding validation evidence, and the cost and environmental implications of testing methods, alongside the lack of guidance for feasible adaptations. Intended for researchers, regulators and standard-setting bodies, it underscores the need for context-appropriate, evidence-based modifications and improved reporting practices to support reliable medicine quality monitoring.

Bacterial infections remain a leading cause of mortality among children under five years of age, while the lack of age-appropriate antibiotic formulations continues to limit effective treatment and compromise quality of care, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This policy and practice article presents target product profiles developed by the World Health Organization, as part of the paediatric drug optimization exercise, to guide the research and development of paediatric formulations of azithromycin and nitrofurantoin, two priority antibiotics identified in the WHO list of essential medicines for children.

The article describes the methodological approach used to define optimal and minimum product characteristics, including dosage strength, pharmaceutical form, safety, efficacy, palatability, stability and packaging requirements. It outlines preferred formulations such as dispersible tablets and orodispersible multiparticulate systems to improve dosing flexibility, acceptability and ease of administration across paediatric age groups. Key challenges addressed include poor palatability of existing liquid formulations, safety concerns related to excipients and limitations in dose precision. The discussion emphasizes the importance of aligning product development with global health needs, regulatory requirements and antimicrobial stewardship principles, and to inform development, regulatory pathways and equitable access. Intended for regulatory authorities, pharmaceutical developers and health programme stakeholders, the profiles provide a framework to support the development of safe, effective and accessible antibiotic formulations tailored to children.

Drawing on lessons from GAP-f’s initial phases, including accelerated access to paediatric HIV medicines, the roadmap presents a coordinated ecosystem approach to improve alignment across the paediatric medicines lifecycle.

The strategy is structured around four interconnected areas of work: portfolio prioritization, clinical research, product development and regulatory processes, and access and delivery. It introduces the “30 by ’30” initiative, which aims to assess priority diseases, accelerate priority medicines and strengthen national paediatric medicine ecosystems by 2030. Building on analyses of medicines included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children and a review of paediatric oncology drug development pipelines, the process aimed to identify priority medicines and formulations requiring further research, development and optimization.

The report describes the methodology, expert consultations and consensus-building process used to establish priority and watch lists of cancer medicines. The document also highlights access challenges affecting selected targeted therapies, outlines key research priorities related to formulation design, safety, bioavailability and regulatory pathways, and proposes actions to improve access to safe, effective and child-friendly cancer medicines globally.

abstract:
Persistent gaps in the availability of age-appropriate antimalarial medicines continue to limit effective treatment and prevention strategies for infants and children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where malaria remains a leading cause of childhood mortality. This meeting report summarizes the outcomes of the paediatric drug optimization (PADO) exercise for malaria convened by WHO and partners in June 2025 to identify priority paediatric formulations requiring accelerated development, improved access or further clinical investigation. The publication examines current therapeutic options for severe malaria, uncomplicated malaria, relapse prevention and chemoprophylaxis, and assesses their suitability for children in terms of dosing flexibility, acceptability, affordability and programmatic use. It also highlights the role of the PADO process in aligning researchers, regulators, manufacturers, funders and procurement agencies around shared priorities for paediatric antimalarial development and access.

The report outlines consensus recommendations generated through discussions among researchers, regulators, clinicians, funders and product development stakeholders. It identifies priority formulations for short-term development, including child-friendly artemisinin-based combinations and dispersible formulations, and highlights products requiring enhanced market access and uptake. Particular attention is given to the need to expand the range of paediatric antimalarial options in response to emerging drug resistance and to support multiple first-line therapy strategies. The document also reviews late-stage antimalarial candidates and long-acting technologies with potential relevance for future paediatric use. In addition, it defines research priorities related to treatment of neonates and infants, optimization of clinical trial design, chemoprevention strategies and evidence generation for vulnerable populations, including children with sickle cell disease.

title: Paediatric drug optimization for epilepsy: meeting report, 1-2 July 2025
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Epilepsy represents a significant global neurological burden affecting millions of children, with persistent gaps in access to appropriate treatment and age-adapted medicines, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. Within the framework of WHO efforts to accelerate access to optimal paediatric formulations, including the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations (GAP-f), this meeting report presents the outcomes of a paediatric drug optimization (PADO) exercise focused on epilepsy.

The document examines current antiseizure medicines, their suitability for paediatric use and key barriers related to availability, affordability and formulation, drawing on a structured review of WHO guidance, including the Model List of Essential Medicines for Children, expert consultation and analysis of the research and development pipeline . It describes consensus-based access, priority and watch lists intended to guide development, regulatory consideration and procurement, and outlines priority research questions, including the need for earlier inclusion of children in clinical trials and improved formulation design. Intended for policymakers, researchers, manufacturers and global health stakeholders, the findings highlight the importance of coordinated action to expand equitable access to safe, effective and child-appropriate epilepsy treatments.

title: Paediatric drug optimization for neglected tropical diseases: meeting report, September 2023
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This meeting report summarizes the World Health Organization (WHO) paediatric drug optimization (PADO) process for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), conducted between October 2022 and September 2023 under the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations (GAP-f). The report describes the evidence review and consensus-building process used to identify priority medicines, preferred paediatric formulations and research needs for four disease areas: schistosomiasis, human African trypanosomiasis, scabies and onchocerciasis, and visceral leishmaniasis. The initiative responds to persistent gaps in age-appropriate formulations, pharmacokinetic evidence and access to medicines for children affected by NTDs, with the aim of accelerating research, development and equitable availability of optimized treatments.

For each disease area, the report presents the current therapeutic landscape, identifies priority formulations and watch-list candidates, and outlines research priorities and implementation considerations. It also discusses challenges related to procurement, financing, regulatory pathways and market sustainability, emphasizing the need for coordinated action to support the development and introduction of child-friendly medicines. The report concludes with cross-cutting recommendations and a consolidated PADO priority list and research agenda intended to guide future investment, product development and policy efforts to improve treatment options for children with neglected tropical diseases.

title: Paediatric research and development landscape for neglected tropical diseases: report on 1999-2022 period
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This technical brief examines the research and development landscape for treatments targeting neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) in children during the period 1999–2022. Drawing on data from the WHO Global Observatory on Health Research and Development and other sources, it analyses the distribution of clinical trials, research priorities, medicine development activities and funding patterns. The report highlights substantial gaps between disease burden and research activity, showing that clinical trials are concentrated in a limited number of countries and are often not aligned with paediatric disease burden. It also identifies challenges affecting the development of paediatric medicines for NTDs, including limited pharmacokinetic data, insufficient financial incentives, low participation of children in clinical trials and the scarcity of age-appropriate formulations.

The document reviews medicines currently in development, assesses the availability of paediatric formulations among essential medicines for NTDs and presents findings from the first WHO Paediatric Drug Optimization exercise for NTDs. Priority products and research needs are identified for schistosomiasis, human African trypanosomiasis, scabies, onchocerciasis and visceral leishmaniasis. The report underscores the need for strengthened research investment, improved monitoring of funding for paediatric products and targeted efforts to accelerate the development and availability of child-appropriate treatments for NTDs.

title: Integrating palliative care and symptom relief into paediatrics: a WHO guide for health-care planners, implementers and managers
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This WHO guide provides practical guidance for health care planners, implementers and managers on integrating paediatric palliative care and symptom relief into health care systems. It addresses the substantial unmet need for prevention and relief of serious health-related suffering among children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and emphasizes that palliative care should be accessible to children with a wide range of serious, complex or life-threatening conditions and integrated with disease prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

The guide proposes an Essential Package of Paediatric Palliative Care and Symptom Relief as the minimum care that should be accessible to any child in any setting, comprising essential medicines, simple equipment, basic social supports and appropriately trained human resources. It outlines a public health approach to implementation through national policies and strategic plans, workforce training, integration across levels of care and home care, and access to essential controlled medicines. These measures aim to improve quality of life for children and families, strengthen health systems and advance universal health coverage.

title: Human resources for health: Equity in specialized care
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract:
Equitable access to specialized care is essential to achieving universal health coverage (UHC), reducing avoidable mortality and disability, and responding to evolving population health needs driven by ageing, noncommunicable diseases, injuries and increasing demand for advanced diagnostics and treatment. Across the WHO South-East Asia Region, the organization, governance, education, production, deployment and retention of specialist health workers significantly influence the equity, quality, efficiency and financial protection offered through health systems. While countries have made substantial progress in expanding the health workforce, inequities in access to specialized care remain a major concern, particularly due to uneven distribution of specialists, urban concentration, private sector growth and migration of specialist doctors. The Region has witnessed significant growth in health workforce availability, with the density of doctors, nurses and midwives increasing by approximately 70% since 2014. While countries have made substantial progress in expanding the health workforce, most countries of the Region currently have an aggregate specialist density significantly below the global average and far below that of Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries. Shortages are particularly notable in anaesthesiology, obstetrics and gynaecology, emergency medicine, surgery, psychiatry, family medicine and other critical specialties. Challenges across the health workforce lifecycle — including workforce planning, training capacity, deployment, retention and performance management — contribute to inequitable access to specialist services. At the same time, countries in the Region have implemented a range of responses to improve equitable access, including strengthening specialist workforce planning, expanding domestic postgraduate education, introducing rural recruitment and retention strategies, implementing financial and non-financial incentives, promoting task-sharing and competency development, and leveraging digital health innovations.
Moving forward there is opportunity to further adopt a comprehensive approach that aligns specialist workforce planning, education, financing, and deployment with current and future population health needs. Priority actions include expanding domestic postgraduate education, strengthening rural and remote retention policies, expanding multidisciplinary team-based care, optimizing task-sharing and scopes of practice, strengthening PHC-based referral and gatekeeping systems, sharing of resources across administrative boundaries, promoting family medicine, and safely scaling digital health and AI-enabled solutions. At the regional level there is opportunity to strengthen cross-country learning and collaboration to advance access to specialist services, including through the establishment of a regional network of health professional regulators and related policymakers. The attached Working Paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting/Meeting of the Subcommittee for Policy and Programme Development and Management (SPPDM) for its review and recommendations. The HLP/SPPDM reviewed the paper, expressed strong support for inclusion of the subject for the Ministerial Round Table, and shared national experiences and challenges including that of international migration. Member States expressed interest in strengthening regional cooperation and capacity building in the area, through establishment of a regional network and sharing of best practices. The HLP/SPPDM made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee: 
Actions by Member States
(1) Enable a comprehensive approach as enumerated in the Working Paper to advance access to quality specialized care aligned with the ongoing PHC-oriented health system transformation.
(2) Share best practices and innovations, as well as strengthen regional collaboration, through the establishment of, and engagement in a regional network of health professional regulators and policymakers.
(3) Participate in the formulation of the Ministerial Declaration on the Agenda item. 
Actions by WHO
(1) Incorporate comments from Member States to further embellish the technical report and Working Paper to be presented at the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee.
(2) Under the leadership of the Government of Timor-Leste, facilitate preparations and discussions among Member States to formulate and develop the Ministerial Declaration and ensure its smooth adoption at the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee
(3) Respond to Member State requests as per their interests in collaborative learning and strengthened cooperation through the establishment of a regional network of health professional regulators and policymakers. This Working Paper along with the HLP Meeting recommendations are placed before the Seventy-ninth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration, as appropriate.

title: Priority interventions to strengthen service delivery for Wilms tumour: Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer technical brief
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Wilms tumour is one of the most common childhood cancers and, with timely diagnosis and access to high-quality care, is associated with high survival rates. This technical brief, developed within the WHO Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer and aligned with its CureAll framework, provides practical, evidence-informed guidance to support policy-makers, hospital managers and cancer control programme managers in planning, financing and coordinating services for children with Wilms tumour across the continuum of care.

The brief identifies seven priority interventions that countries can adapt to their contexts: reducing delayed diagnosis through early detection; improving access to diagnosis and staging; improving access to quality treatment; preventing treatment abandonment; providing adequate supportive care; integrating palliative care; and ensuring survivorship care. For each intervention, it presents the rationale for action, system-level considerations and guiding questions for service organization and delivery. It also addresses the scaling and integration of these interventions within national cancer control plans, essential health service packages and universal health coverage schemes to improve access, quality and equity of care.

title: Standards for donor human milk banking
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This document presents the World Health Organization’s global standards for donor human milk banking, developed to ensure the safety, quality and ethical management of donor human milk used for vulnerable infants when their mother’s own milk is unavailable or insufficient. Donor human milk is recommended for preterm and low-birthweight infants as an important intervention to support survival, growth and development. The standards were developed through systematic reviews, consideration of ethical issues and expert consensus, with the aim of providing harmonized, evidence-based guidance for policymakers, health systems and milk bank operators.

The publication outlines recommended practices across the donor human milk banking pathway, including donor recruitment, remuneration, screening, education and support; collection, storage, handling and processing of milk; pooling, tracking and tracing systems; treatment and microbiological testing of donor milk; and quality assurance measures. Particular emphasis is placed on protecting breastfeeding, safeguarding donor and recipient health, ensuring traceability, and maintaining microbiological safety while preserving the nutritional and immunological value of human milk. The standards are intended to support equitable access to safe donor human milk and strengthen integration of milk banking within maternal, newborn and child health programmes.

title: Global status report on cancer 2026: the future we choose together
authors: World Health Organization; International Agency for Research on Cancer
abstract:
The Global status report on cancer 2026 provides a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of cancer, progress in cancer prevention and control, and the systemic challenges that continue to limit equitable outcomes. Presenting new data on the burden of disease, the capacity of health systems to respond, and the lived experiences of people affected by cancer, the report examines trends in incidence, mortality, survival, risk factors and health system performance, as well as the human, social and economic consequences of cancer. It reviews implementation across the cancer continuum, including prevention, early detection, diagnosis, treatment, palliative care and survivorship, highlighting persistent disparities between and within countries and the gap between ambition and action.

The report analyses the factors that drive progress and those that impede effective implementation, emphasizing the importance of integrated, people-centred approaches, universal health coverage, robust monitoring systems and meaningful engagement of affected communities. It highlights the coexistence of scientific advances and persistent inequities in who benefits from them and proposes a framework for future action based on three strategic shifts—better capabilities, better protections and better value. Seven recommendations guide governments, international organizations and other stakeholders in strengthening cancer control and advancing more equitable outcomes worldwide.

title: TDR annual report 2025: building local research solutions to improve global health
authors: World Health Organization; UNICEF/UNDP/World Bank/WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases
abstract:
The TDR annual report 2025 presents an overview of the activities, achievements and strategic directions of the UNICEF/UNDP/World Bank/WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR), focusing on its role in supporting research and capacity strengthening to address infectious diseases of poverty. The report outlines how TDR contributes to improving health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries by promoting implementation research, fostering innovation and facilitating the translation of evidence into practical interventions. It situates this work within the broader global health context, emphasizing persistent challenges such as disease burden, inequities in access to care and evolving environmental and epidemiological threats.

Structured around key thematic areas aligned with the TDR Strategy 2024–2029, the report highlights research efforts addressing disease control and elimination, climate change impacts on health, epidemics and outbreaks, and resistance to treatment and control agents. It also describes initiatives to strengthen research capacity, leadership and global collaboration through training programmes, networks and partnerships. The report underscores TDR’s emphasis on locally led, context-specific research and a One Health approach, while illustrating how evidence generation supports policy development, health system resilience and equitable access to effective interventions.

title: National guideline development and adaptation, Egypt
authors: Kheirandish, Mehrnaz; Tamim, Malika A; Rashidian, Arash; El-Asady, Riham; Al Qasseer, Naeema; Gad El Kareem, Gasser; Lotayef, Mohamed Mostafa; Youssif, Mohammed Mourad; Akl, Elie A; Fordf, Nathan; Garnerg, Paul
abstract:
Efforts to strengthen health systems and achieve universal health coverage increasingly depend on the development and use of high-quality, evidence-based clinical and public health guidelines. This paper describes the establishment of a national programme for guideline development and adaptation in Egypt, initiated in response to the country’s 2018 health reform law mandating equitable and effective care.

The article outlines a collaborative approach led by the Ministry of Health and Population, the Egyptian Health Council and the World Health Organization, including a situation analysis, structured capacity-building activities and the development of a national roadmap. It describes the application of standardized methods, including GRADE-based approaches, for prioritizing, developing and adapting guidelines, and highlights improvements in coordination, role clarity and harmonization across institutions and professional groups. Implementation resulted in the training of over 200 stakeholders and the publication of multiple clinical and public health guidelines. The experience underscores the importance of sustained political commitment, stakeholder engagement and investment in national technical capacity, while identifying challenges such as reliance on external expertise, limited resources and institutional constraints. The findings highlight the need for ongoing monitoring, evaluation and institutional strengthening, and offer practical insights for policy-makers seeking to establish similar programmes in comparable settings.

title: Target product profiles for new antibacterial agents: severe multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, antibiotic-resistant Gram-positive infections in immunosuppressed and critically ill patients, and community-acquired and health care-associated bacterial meningitis
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This World Health Organization (WHO) report presents target product profiles (TPPs) for new antibacterial agents for the treatment of severe multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, antibiotic-resistant Gram-positive infections in immunosuppressed and critically ill patients, and community-acquired and health care-associated bacterial meningitis.

The TPPs outline the desired characteristics of novel antibiotics, including intended use, target populations, pharmacokinetics, safety, efficacy, route of administration, stability, and considerations related to access and affordability, to support research and development (R&D) of products addressing the most urgent public health needs posed by antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

Building on previous WHO antibacterial TPPs, the report aligns product development with the WHO bacterial priority pathogens list (BPPL) 2024 and evidence from global antibacterial pipeline analyses. It prioritizes syndromes with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and highlights the importance of integrating equity, stewardship and regulatory considerations, as well as strengthening public–private partnerships to accelerate development and ensure equitable access to new antibiotics.

title: Antifungal agents in clinical and preclinical development: overview and analysis
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This report presents the first WHO analysis of antifungal agents in clinical and preclinical development worldwide. It reviews systemic antifungal drugs targeting WHO fungal priority pathogens, including newly approved products, agents undergoing clinical evaluation, repurposed medicines and compounds in preclinical development. The publication examines the extent to which the current antifungal pipeline addresses infections caused by critical, high- and medium-priority fungal pathogens identified in the WHO fungal priority pathogens list. It also evaluates innovation potential using criteria such as new chemical classes, novel targets, mechanisms of action and evidence of reduced cross-resistance.

The document highlights major limitations in the current antifungal arsenal, including toxicity, drug–drug interactions, prolonged treatment courses and limited paediatric formulations, alongside the growing challenge of antifungal resistance. It analyses trends in clinical and preclinical research and development, identifies gaps in therapeutic coverage for priority pathogens, and discusses scientific, regulatory and economic barriers affecting antifungal innovation. The publication is intended to support policy-makers, researchers, developers and funders in prioritizing research and investment toward urgently needed antifungal therapies and improved global preparedness against invasive fungal diseases.

title: Second meeting of the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group working group on access to safe, efficacious and quality-assured health products for neglected tropical diseases: virtual meeting, 19 September 2023

abstract:
This report summarizes the discussions and recommendations of the second virtual meeting of the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group working group on access to safe, efficacious and quality-assured health products for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), held on 19 September 2023. The meeting reviewed progress since 2022 in advancing the WHO NTD road map 2021–2030, with particular emphasis on procurement and supply chain management, drug efficacy monitoring, paediatric drug optimization and assessment of access and logistics. Participants examined current challenges affecting the availability of medicines and diagnostics, including supply constraints, procurement coordination, funding limitations and the need to strengthen domestic procurement mechanisms.

The report presents updates from technical subgroups and ongoing WHO initiatives, including monitoring of anthelminthic drug efficacy, priorities for paediatric formulations of NTD medicines, and the development of a global gap assessment tool to identify barriers to access. The Working Group reaffirmed the importance of expanding drug efficacy monitoring across additional NTDs, revising existing WHO protocols where needed, strengthening coordination among procurement partners, refining the mandate of the procurement and supply chain management subgroup, and promoting sustainable approaches to forecasting, financing and access to quality-assured health products in endemic countries.

title: Roadmap towards ending TB in children and adolescents
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This third edition of the Roadmap towards ending TB in children and adolescents updates the 2013 and 2018 editions and provides a strategic framework to accelerate progress towards global tuberculosis (TB) targets. The document reviews the burden of TB among children, adolescents, and, for the first time, pregnant and post-partum women, highlighting persistent gaps in case detection, preventive treatment, and access to care despite important advances in policy, diagnostics, treatment options, and service delivery. It assesses progress achieved since the 2018 Roadmap, including the development of child-friendly medicines, updated WHO guidance, improved diagnostic approaches, strengthened advocacy, and expanded research efforts.

Building on lessons learned and remaining challenges, the Roadmap identifies priority actions for the next five years to reduce TB-related morbidity and mortality and improve equitable access to prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. It emphasizes political leadership and accountability, multisectoral engagement, implementation of people-, family- and community-centred approaches within primary health care, and strengthened data systems and research. Aligned with universal health coverage and the WHO End TB Strategy, the publication aims to support countries and partners in addressing the specific needs of vulnerable populations and advancing efforts to end TB among children and adolescents.

title: Research and development landscape for childhood cancer: a 2023 perspective
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This report summarizes the 2023 research and development (R&D) landscape for childhood cancer using data from the WHO Global Observatory on Health R&D to identify major gaps and barriers affecting the development, evaluation and access to medicines and other interventions for children with cancer. It highlights the marked imbalance between the global burden of childhood cancer, which falls predominantly on low- and middle-income countries, and the geographical distribution of clinical research, investment and innovation. The document emphasizes the need for greater investment in paediatric oncology research, child-specific clinical trials, implementation research and product development that reflects the unique biology of childhood cancers, together with the development of age-appropriate formulations and stronger research capacity in resource-limited settings.

The report also examines regulatory, funding and health-system challenges that delay access to effective therapies, including lengthy approval processes, limited paediatric indications and inequities in access to emerging treatments. It outlines examples of regulatory approaches and international collaboration that could accelerate the development and approval of paediatric cancer medicines while reducing unnecessary duplication of research. The publication concludes that strengthening the global R&D ecosystem, improving transparency in research funding, aligning regulatory processes, and investing in health-system readiness are essential to ensure equitable access to evidence-based innovations and improved outcomes for children with cancer worldwide.

title: Guidance for best practices for clinical trials
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This guidance document provides recommendations and best practices for strengthening the design, conduct, oversight and enabling environment of clinical trials globally. Developed in response to World Health Assembly resolution WHA75.8 (2022), it aims to improve the generation of high-quality evidence on health interventions, reduce research waste and support equitable access to safe and effective innovations. The publication addresses scientific, ethical and operational considerations for clinical trials across diverse settings and intervention types, with particular emphasis on randomized clinical trials, inclusivity, participant protection, transparency and proportionate risk-based approaches to trial oversight and quality management.

The guidance also examines persistent barriers affecting the global clinical trial ecosystem, including inefficient regulatory and approval processes, inadequate funding, underrepresentation of certain populations, and inequities affecting low- and middle-income countries. It outlines strategies to strengthen national and international clinical trial capacity through coordinated governance, sustained investment, community engagement and streamlined regulatory pathways. title: Improved influenza vaccines: full value vaccine assessment
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Seasonal influenza remains a major global public health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality each year and underscoring the need for more effective and durable vaccines. This report presents a full value of vaccine assessment of improved seasonal influenza vaccines, providing a comprehensive, evidence-based analysis of their potential health, economic and societal value. It aims to inform decision-making across the vaccine development and implementation continuum by synthesizing data on disease burden, vaccine innovation and public health impact, and by aligning with WHO preferred product characteristics for next-generation influenza vaccines. The assessment is intended for vaccine developers, funders, policy-makers, national immunization programmes and other stakeholders involved in influenza prevention and control.

The document applies a structured, multi-component methodology to examine the global need for improved vaccines, the development pipeline and emerging technologies, and criteria influencing country-level adoption decisions. It includes modelling of health and economic outcomes, demonstrating the potential of improved vaccines to reduce infections, hospitalizations and deaths, and to be cost-effective or cost-saving under specific conditions. The report also analyses market dynamics, financing considerations and barriers to implementation, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and identifies key enablers such as strengthened surveillance, supportive policies and integrated immunization strategies. It provides evidence-informed insights to guide investment, policy development and equitable access to improved influenza vaccines.

This document provides strategic guidance for the development and implementation of quality of care programmes for maternal, newborn and child health within national health systems. Building on the experience of the Network for Improving Quality of Care for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health, it presents the updated LALA+ framework—leadership, action, learning, accountability and measurement—refined in 2023 based on implementation experience. The publication is intended for national and subnational policy-makers, programme managers, health professionals and partners involved in strengthening quality of care and advancing progress towards universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals.

It details the strategic objectives, expected outputs and associated deliverables, organized across structures, processes and capacities at macro, meso and micro levels. It also emphasizes alignment with global initiatives and frameworks, including primary health care and maternal, newborn and child health strategies. By promoting a whole-system, country-led approach supported by data, learning and accountability mechanisms, the guidance aims to strengthen health system performance, improve equitable access to high-quality, people-centred care, and accelerate reductions in preventable maternal, newborn and child morbidity and mortality.

This guidance  presents a structured competency and outcomes framework to support the development of competency-based education in adolescent health and development, serving as a reference for curriculum content and assessable learning outcomes in both pre-service and in-service training.

The document describes a comprehensive set of competencies, behaviours, knowledge and skills required of health workers, adapted from the broader framework for universal health coverage and organized across key domains such as people-centred care, communication, decision-making and evidence-informed practice. title: Target product profiles for small molecule or engineered antibody therapeutics for treatment of snakebite envenoming
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This document presents World Health Organization (WHO) target product profiles (TPPs) for small molecule therapeutics and engineered antibody therapeutics for the treatment of snakebite envenoming, a neglected tropical disease responsible for substantial mortality and morbidity worldwide.

The TPPs are intended to guide research and development, regulatory assessment and procurement of new treatments by defining optimal and minimal characteristics related to safety, efficacy, quality, accessibility and cost-effectiveness. They address key unmet needs associated with existing antivenoms, including limited availability, species specificity, safety concerns and challenges in timely access, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

The document outlines use-case scenarios for both health facility–based treatment and pre-hospital emergency care, and specifies product requirements across manufacturing, performance and operational domains. It highlights emerging therapeutic approaches, including small molecule inhibitors and engineered antibody technologies, as promising complements or alternatives to conventional antivenoms.

title: Report of existing technologies used to screen and detect substandard and falsified medical products
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This report presents the findings of a WHO survey on technologies used by Member States to screen and detect substandard and falsified medical products, including medicines and vaccines within the supply chain. The publication examines existing regulatory frameworks, operational procedures, laboratory practices and detection technologies used in both field and laboratory settings. It also analyses the roles and responsibilities of national regulatory authorities and other stakeholders involved in quality control and surveillance activities. The report aims to support the future development of WHO guidance on the selection and use of technologies for detecting substandard and falsified medical products.

The survey findings highlight significant variation among Member States in legal provisions, technical capacity, testing approaches and availability of detection technologies. Commonly used laboratory technologies include high-performance liquid chromatography, UV/VIS spectrophotometry, infrared spectroscopy and thin-layer chromatography, while portable field technologies include MiniLab systems, handheld spectroscopy devices and paper analytical devices. The report also identifies major implementation challenges, including insufficient funding, limited technical expertise, immature regulatory systems and gaps in supply chain regulation, all of which affect the sustainable use of detection technologies and the timely identification of poor-quality medical products.

abstract:
This activity report presents findings from the World Health Organization’s Global Surveillance and Monitoring System (GSMS) for substandard and falsified medical products during the period August 2017–December 2021. It examines the scale, scope and characteristics of reported incidents worldwide, describes trends in affected product categories and highlights the role of the GSMS in supporting the prevention, detection and response to threats posed by substandard and falsified medical products. The report documents a continued increase in recorded incidents involving essential medicines, vaccines and in vitro diagnostic medical devices, and outlines challenges faced by Member States, including limited technical capacity, weak governance, inadequate reporting systems and insufficient international information exchange.

The report analyses the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on medical product supply chains and demand, including the emergence of substandard and falsified products associated with the pandemic response. It reviews risks affecting different therapeutic categories and diagnostic devices, identifies key drivers and facilitators of the problem, and assesses gaps in regulatory oversight, market surveillance and reporting. The report emphasizes the need for strengthened regulatory systems, sustainable national reporting mechanisms, enhanced cooperation among regulators and law-enforcement authorities, greater public awareness and improved international collaboration to protect public health and ensure access to safe, effective and quality-assured medical products.

title: SEA/RC65/10 - Reports of WHO global working/advisory groups: substandards/spurious/falsely-labelled/falsified/counterfeit medical products and strengthening drug regulatory authorities
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: The issue of substandard/spurious/falsely-labelled/falsified/counterfeit medical products (SSFFC) has been discussed at the World Health Assembly since 2010 following the seizure in 2008 of generic medicines in transit through the Netherlands on the basis of infringement of intellectual property. Since then the lack of a uniform definition of “counterfeit” medical products and certain activities of International Medical Products Anti-counterfeiting Task Force (IMPACT) set up to combat counterfeit medical products in 2006, have engaged the attention of Member States. IMPACT and WHO’s involvement was discussed at the Sixty-third World Health Assembly in 2010. The World Health Assembly decided “to establish a time-limited and results-oriented working group on substandard/spurious/falsely-labelled/falsified/counterfeit medical products comprised of and open to all Member States” to examine inter alia WHO’s role in ensuring availability of quality, safe, efficacious and affordable medical products and WHO’s relationship with IMPACT. The Inter-Governmental Working Group (IGWG) presented its report to the Sixty-fifth World Health Assembly in 2012. Indonesia was Vice-Chair in both the IGWG meetings of 2011. There is unanimous support for WHO’s role in measures to ensure the availability of good quality, safe, efficacious and affordable medical products and concern was also expressed at the lack of sufficient financing for WHO’s work in this area. The IGWG recommendations are incorporated into Resolution WHA65.19 which urges Member States to: (1) voluntarily participate and collaborate with the proposed Member State Mechanism; (2) provide sufficient financial resources (US$ 2 370 000–3 230 000 in 2012–2013) to strengthen the work of the Secretariat in this area; and requests the Director-General to:  support the proposed Member State Mechanism;  assist Member States in building capacity to prevent and control SSFFC, which will necessarily involve strengthening drug regulatory authorities. At the Sixty-fifth World Health Assembly, 33 delegations made statements on SSFFC. A number of delegations emphasized the importance of WHO’s involvement in combating SSFFC and expressed their concern about the funding gap. It is important that all Member States participate, and Member States of SEA Region adequately engage in this proposed new Member State Mechanism. Member States may like to consider their support to improving access to safe, efficacious and affordable medicines of good quality by strengthening drug regulatory authorities, incorporating public health safeguards and not decreasing access through intellectual property policies. The High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting held in the Regional Office in New Delhi from 3 to 5 July 2012, reviewed the working paper and made the following recommendations: Actions by Member States (1) To participate in the proposed Member State Mechanism. (2) To undertake in-depth assessments of the capacity of the national drug regulatory authorities (NDRAs) in combating SSFFC. (3) To provide sufficient human and financial resources to strengthen the capacity of NDRAs in combating SSFFC. Actions by WHO-SEARO (1) To provide technical support to Member States to undertake in-depth assessments of the capacity of the NDRAs in combating SSFFC. (2) To develop, based on evidence from the assessment in Member States, a regional medium-term strategic plan to combat SSFFC. (3) To explore the possibility of establishing a mechanism for bulk purchase of drugs and vaccines of assured quality particularly for Member States who depend on importation of drugs and vaccines. (4) To report the progress and outcome of the implementation of the regional mediumterm strategic plan to the Sixty-eighth meeting of the Regional Committee. The working paper has been revised to include discussions from the HLP Meeting and is submitted with the HLP Meeting recommendations to the Sixty-fifth Session of the Regional Committee for its consideration.

abstract: Understanding the factors that operate during pregnancy, delivery and postpartum is the key to success in the prevention of maternal mortality. This cross-sectional survey in Jordan for the years 2007-2008 aimed to identify the role of substandard care and delays in maternal deaths. All maternal deaths among women aged 15-49 years over this period [n = 76] were investigated retrospectively through file review and household interviews in all hospitals [n =102] and forensic medicine departments in Jordan; elements of substandard care and delays at hospital, home and transport levels were evaluated. Substandard care accounted for 52.6% of deaths, delay in seeking care 55.3%, delay in transport 15,8% and delay in hospital care 17.1%. Women who did not recognize the danger signs of pregnancy [OR 6.32], refused medical advice to terminate the pregnancy [OR 1.78] or at a gestational age > 37 weeks [OR 1.85] were significantly more likely to delay seeking care, as were those with larger mean family size

title: Global traditional medicine strategy 2025-2034

abstract:
Growing global reliance on traditional, complementary and integrative medicine (TCIM) highlights the need for coherent policies to ensure its safe, effective and equitable contribution to health systems. This strategy outlines a comprehensive framework to guide Member States and stakeholders in strengthening the role of TCIM in achieving universal health coverage and improving population health and well-being, in alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals and relevant international commitments.

It presents a vision of universal access to people-centred TCIM and defines strategic objectives focused on strengthening the evidence base, establishing appropriate regulatory mechanisms, integrating TCIM into health systems and optimizing its cross-sectoral value. The document describes guiding principles such as evidence-based practice, health equity, sustainability, respect for Indigenous Peoples’ rights and culturally appropriate care. It further examines key areas including research development, regulatory standards for products and practitioners, integration across the continuum of care and life course, and mechanisms to protect and promote traditional medical knowledge. Developed through an extensive consultative process involving Member States, experts and diverse stakeholders, the strategy also underscores the importance of addressing misinformation and ensuring that all practices are grounded in robust scientific evidence. Intended for policy-makers, health authorities and partners, it supports the design and implementation of national plans adapted to local contexts, while promoting global collaboration, monitoring and evaluation to ensure the safe and effective use of TCIM.

Intended for policy-makers, regulators, researchers and health system planners, the publication provides an important baseline for monitoring implementation of the WHO global traditional medicine strategy 2025–2034 and supports the development of safe, effective and culturally responsive traditional, complementary and integrative medicine within national health systems.

title: Universal health coverage partnership annual report 2023: strengthening health systems to achieve universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Persistent gaps in access to essential health services and financial protection underscore the need for sustained investment and coordinated action to strengthen health systems and advance universal health coverage (UHC). This report presents the 2023 annual results of the Universal Health Coverage Partnership (UHC-P), WHO’s largest platform for international cooperation on UHC, which supports countries through a primary health care (PHC)-oriented approach and a multi-donor financing mechanism.

The report synthesizes country-level activities and achievements across more than 125 countries, structured around WHO’s Triple Billion targets: expanding access to essential services, improving protection from health emergencies and enhancing population health and well-being. It highlights progress in governance, health financing, workforce capacity, access to medicines and strengthening health information systems, delivered through policy dialogue, technical assistance and the deployment of in-country health policy advisors. Drawing on country office data, regional analyses and case studies, it identifies key enabling factors such as political commitment, partner coordination and capacity-building, alongside persistent challenges related to equity, sustainable financing and system resilience. Intended for policy-makers, development partners and health system stakeholders, it informs strategic planning and supports accelerated progress towards UHC.
