title: The path towards universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization; Inter-Parliamentary Union
abstract:
This handbook, jointly developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), provides practical guidance for parliamentarians on advancing universal health coverage (UHC) through their legislative, budgetary and oversight functions. It explains the concept and importance of UHC as a practical expression of the right to health and a key target of the Sustainable Development Goals, emphasizing equitable access to quality health services, financial protection and the principle of leaving no one behind. The publication outlines the essential elements of strong, people-centred health systems and the role of primary health care in achieving sustainable progress towards UHC.

The publication examines how parliaments can support UHC by developing and reviewing legislation, strengthening health financing, ensuring accountability and monitoring implementation. It presents practical actions for members of parliament, discusses legal and institutional frameworks, and highlights approaches to improving governance, transparency and equitable access to health services. Drawing on WHO guidance, international commitments and country experiences, the publication serves as a resource for promoting evidence-informed policies and reinforcing parliamentary leadership in the pursuit of universal health coverage.

title: Regional strategy on universal health coverage
abstract: There has been strong and consistent commitment to improving equity in health through universal coverage in the Region as well as global level from WHO and Member States. An overall financing strategy towards achieving this goal has been developed for the Asia-Pacific Region jointly by South-East Asia Region Office and Western-Pacific Region Office. Further, these regional priorities will be a focus of the forthcoming 2010 World Health Report, Financing for universal coverage.Key challenges to financing for universal coverage in the Region are high and potentially impoverishing out-of-pocket spending on health; a large and poor informal sector that is most vulnerable to the high cost of access to care; a large and mostly unregulated private sector that dominates provision of care; and an increasing burden of non-communicable disease requiring high-cost individual care.There are three choices in progress towards universal coverage that health financing reform needs to consider: priority population to be reached with a chosen benefit package at a feasible public subsidy. A practical approach to shift from out-of-pocket payments towards equity and universal coverage is a step-by-step move, first to an intermediate stage of a mix of community initiatives to protect the informal sector and social insurance for the formal sector with general government revenues focusing on public health and the poor; and, a next stage that consolidates community and social insurance into national level social protection schemes with continued public investment in public health and target population.In-depth technical assessments of the potential of this approach to sustainable financing for universal coverage in Member States is recommended to formulate a strategy for the Region to be considered by the Sixty-fourth Regional Committee in 2011 for furtheraction.The attached working paper is submitted to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. The recommendations made by the HLP Meeting will be submitted to the Sixty-third Session of the Regional Committee for its consideration.

title: Digital health diplomacy and universal health coverage
authors: Barbosa da Silva, Jarbas; Valdez, Mary Lou; Sealey-Thomas, Rhonda; Galiano, Socorro Gross; Garcia-Saisó, Sebastian; Huerta, Piedad; McInnis, Luis Jimenez; Teixeira, Mariana Faria; Marti, Myrna; Haddad, Ana Estela; D’Agostino, Marcelo
abstract:
This perspective article examines the role of digital health diplomacy in advancing universal health coverage and reducing global inequities in access to digital health technologies. The authors argue that rapid digital transformation, accelerated by the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, has created new opportunities to improve health service delivery, access and efficiency through innovations such as telehealth, electronic health records and artificial intelligence. At the same time, persistent disparities in digital infrastructure, connectivity, digital literacy and policy development continue to limit equitable access, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The article presents digital health diplomacy as a mechanism for fostering international cooperation, aligning health and foreign policy agendas, and supporting the equitable deployment of digital health solutions across borders.

Drawing on examples from the Pan American Health Organization, the Group of 20 and global responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors highlight the importance of multistakeholder collaboration involving governments, international organizations, civil society and the private sector. Key priorities include strengthening digital public infrastructure, developing frameworks for data sharing and governance, promoting digital literacy, supporting public–private partnerships and ensuring inclusive access to digital health innovations. The article concludes that digital health diplomacy is essential for bridging the global digital divide and building resilient, accessible and equitable health systems capable of supporting progress towards universal health coverage and broader sustainable development goals.

title: SDGs and progress towards universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: Agenda item 8.6 for the Seventieth Session of the Regional Committee has two sub-items: (i) Strengthening primary health care and health workforce, and (ii) Annual progress monitoring of UHC and SDGs. Heath is centrally placed in the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. Universal health coverage (UHC) is recognized as a unifying platform for making progress on Sustainable Development Goal 3 for health. The momentum around the SDGs and UHC has created new demands and opportunities for strengthening primary health care. The need for services for maternal and child health and communicable diseases continues. At the same time, ageing populations and noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are putting new demands on all levels of care, especially frontline services. Monitoring progress on UHC and the SDGs will help identify bottlenecks and make any needed adjustments to policies and plans. New frontline service delivery models are being developed in the South-East Asia Region. Care needs to become more “integrated” as lifelong health conditions become more common. New service delivery models need to be closely linked with strategies to strengthen the health workforce, and discussions on financing. Partnerships with nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and the private sector may help to address some aspects of exclusion, and these actors need to be brought into discussions about strengthening primary-level care. Strengthening frontline services involves multiple interventions within and beyond the health sector. It, therefore, requires political leadership. Better data and more syntheses of evidence, and experience with different service delivery models and new skill-mix approaches are urgently needed. This Region is already taking action on monitoring the SDGs and UHC. There are some clear priorities: setting national health SDG targets; improving equity monitoring; strengthening civil registration and vital statistics; and maintaining regular reviews of progress.

title: Trend analysis and modelling of universal health coverage, Ethiopia
authors: Assefa, Yibeltal; Gelaw, Yalemzewod Assefa; Endalamaw, Aklilu; Wolka, Eskinder; Zewdie, Antene
abstract:
Universal health coverage (UHC) remains a central global health objective, yet many countries face persistent challenges in achieving equitable access to essential services. This research article examines the attainability of the UHC service coverage target of 80% by 2030, using Ethiopia as a case study, through analysis of historical trends and projections of the universal health service coverage index and estimates the probability of achieving the target.

The study analyses changes in the composite UHC index and its subindices between 2000 and 2021, and applies Bayesian projection modelling and simulation techniques to estimate future trajectories up to 2030 and 2040. Findings indicate a trajectory marked by early gains followed by recent stagnation, with steady improvements until 2015 and limited progress thereafter. Projections suggest that coverage will reach approximately 64.7% by 2030, falling short of the global target, with particularly limited gains in noncommunicable diseases and service capacity. Simulation results show that even substantial increases in health system inputs, including financing, infrastructure and workforce, would yield only modest improvements in coverage. The article highlights the need for structural reforms, strengthened governance and integrated health system approaches to accelerate progress and provides an analytical framework to inform context-specific strategies towards achieving UHC.

title: Rehabilitation in health financing: opportunities on the way to universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This guidance examines how health financing can be leveraged to strengthen rehabilitation services as an essential component of universal health coverage. Drawing on a review of evidence, country practices and key informant interviews, it analyses the financing of rehabilitation across the core health financing functions of revenue collection, pooling, purchasing and governance. The publication describes current financing arrangements, identifies common challenges that limit access and financial protection, and highlights opportunities to improve the integration of rehabilitation into health systems. It also discusses the needs of populations requiring rehabilitation and the organization and delivery of rehabilitation services.

The document provides policy considerations and practical approaches for decision-makers to strengthen financing for rehabilitation through adequate public funding, effective risk pooling, inclusion of rehabilitation in health benefits packages, strategic purchasing and improved governance. Case studies illustrate selected country experiences in financing rehabilitation services. The guidance emphasizes the importance of evidence-informed planning, intersectoral coordination, stronger health information systems and sustained investment to improve equitable access to quality rehabilitation services while reducing financial hardship, particularly for vulnerable populations.

title: Social participation for universal health coverage: technical paper
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This technical paper examines social participation as a means of advancing equitable progress towards universal health coverage by enabling people, communities and civil society to influence health-related decision-making across the policy cycle and at all levels of the system. Drawing on WHO guidance and a multistakeholder consultation process, it highlights the role of meaningful participation in promoting equity, strengthening trust and health system resilience, and advancing transparency and accountability. It also notes that country approaches are often ad hoc, fragmented or tokenistic, limiting the influence of participatory processes on decisions.

The publication identifies priority actions for Member States to institutionalize social participation. These include strengthening government capacities to design and implement meaningful participation; securing equitable, diverse and inclusive representation; ensuring that participatory mechanisms inform decision-making throughout the policy cycle; systematizing and sustaining participation, including through legal frameworks; providing adequate, stable and predictable financing; strengthening civil society capacities and resources; and routinely using data and evidence to evaluate participatory processes and their impact on decisions.

title: Tracking universal health coverage: 2025 global monitoring report
authors: World Health Organization; International Bank for Reconstruction and Development/The World Bank
abstract:
This global monitoring report 2025 provides a comprehensive assessment of progress towards universal health coverage (UHC), defined as access to quality health services without financial hardship. It presents the first round of global, regional and country-level analyses based on revised Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators 3.8.1 and 3.8.2, which measure service coverage through the UHC service coverage index (SCI) and financial hardship related to out-of-pocket (OOP) health spending. Drawing on data from 2000 onwards, the report examines trends, inequalities and methodological changes in monitoring UHC.

Findings indicate that, although progress has been made in expanding service coverage and reducing financial hardship, gains have slowed during the SDG period and remain uneven across and within countries. Large gaps persist, with billions lacking access to essential services and many experiencing financial strain, particularly among poorer and vulnerable populations. Progress has been driven mainly by improvements in infectious disease control, while advances in noncommunicable diseases have lagged. The report highlights structural challenges, including high reliance on OOP spending, especially for medicines, and emphasizes the need for strengthened public financing, primary health care and multisectoral approaches to accelerate equitable progress towards UHC.

title: Tracking universal health coverage: 2023 global monitoring report
authors: World Health Organization; International Bank for Reconstruction and Development; World Bank
abstract:
This global monitoring report assesses progress towards universal health coverage (UHC) within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals, focusing on trends in service coverage and financial protection. Drawing on the latest available data from WHO and the World Bank, it analyses two core indicators: SDG 3.8.1 on coverage of essential health services and SDG 3.8.2 on financial hardship associated with out-of-pocket health spending. The report is intended to inform policy-makers, health system planners and international stakeholders involved in monitoring and advancing UHC.

The publication examines global, regional and country-level trends from 2000 onwards, highlighting patterns of progress, persistent inequalities and emerging challenges. It reviews changes in access to key health services, disparities across population groups, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on health systems, and analyses the joint evolution of service coverage and financial protection. The findings indicate that gains in service coverage have slowed in recent years, while financial hardship has increased, leaving a substantial proportion of the global population without adequate access to essential services. The report underscores the need for strengthened investment, policy action and health system reforms to accelerate progress towards equitable and sustainable UHC.

abstract:
This global monitoring report provides a comprehensive assessment of progress towards universal health coverage (UHC) within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals. Drawing on data compiled by WHO and the World Bank, it analyses two core dimensions: SDG indicator 3.8.1 on coverage of essential health services and SDG indicator 3.8.2 on financial protection, measured through out-of-pocket health spending. The report is intended to support policy-makers, health system planners and international stakeholders in monitoring trends, identifying gaps and informing national policy responses to advance UHC.

The analysis shows that service coverage has improved globally since 2000, with gains driven particularly by interventions targeting infectious diseases and maternal and child health, although progress remains uneven across regions and population groups. At the same time, the incidence of catastrophic health spending has increased, and a substantial proportion of the global population continues to face financial hardship when accessing care. The report also examines the joint evolution of service coverage and financial protection, highlighting persistent inequalities both between and within countries. The COVID-19 pandemic has further disrupted essential health services and is likely to exacerbate financial barriers to care. The report highlights the need for strengthened health systems based on primary health care, increased public investment and improved data systems to accelerate equitable and sustainable progress towards UHC.

title: Tracking universal health coverage: 2017 global monitoring report
authors: World Health Organization; World Bank
abstract:
This report provides a comprehensive assessment of global progress towards universal health coverage (UHC) in the context of the Sustainable Development Goals. Drawing on joint work by WHO and the World Bank, it presents a monitoring framework based on two core dimensions: coverage of essential health services (SDG indicator 3.8.1) and financial protection (SDG indicator 3.8.2). The report describes the development of an index of essential service coverage derived from tracer and proxy indicators across key health areas, and examines patterns of access, equity and health system performance across countries.

The analysis indicates that, despite improvements in service coverage since 2000, at least half of the world’s population still lacks access to essential health services. Significant disparities persist between and within countries, particularly affecting poorer populations. At the same time, a substantial number of people experience financial hardship due to out-of-pocket health spending, including both catastrophic and impoverishing expenditures. The report emphasizes the importance of jointly monitoring service coverage and financial protection to capture unmet need and inequities. It highlights the need for strengthened health systems, improved data availability and country-led monitoring efforts to support equitable progress towards UHC and inform policy development.

abstract:
This report presents the first global assessment of progress towards universal health coverage (UHC), within the evolving context of the Sustainable Development Goals. Developed jointly by WHO and the World Bank, it introduces a monitoring framework based on two core dimensions: coverage of essential health services and financial protection. It aims to demonstrate how UHC can be measured using a set of tracer indicators and available data sources, and is intended for policy-makers, researchers and stakeholders involved in health system planning and evaluation.

The report examines global and regional patterns in service coverage across key areas such as reproductive, maternal and child health, infectious diseases, and selected determinants of health, as well as trends in financial protection, including catastrophic and impoverishing health expenditures. The findings indicate that, while access to essential services has improved in many settings, substantial gaps remain, with at least hundreds of millions of people lacking access to basic care and significant inequalities persisting within and between countries. Financial hardship associated with out-of-pocket payments continues to affect a considerable proportion of the population. The report highlights data limitations and methodological challenges in monitoring UHC, and emphasizes the need for strengthened health information systems, improved equity-focused measurement, and integrated monitoring approaches to support progress towards equitable and sustainable UHC.

title: Long-term care for older people: package for universal health coverage

abstract:
This WHO publication presents a package of long-term care (LTC) interventions for older people designed to support countries in developing, strengthening and expanding LTC systems as part of universal health coverage. Responding to population ageing, increasing prevalence of chronic conditions and growing care needs, the document addresses the challenges associated with insufficient formal LTC services, workforce shortages, reliance on unpaid carers and financial hardship experienced by older people and their families. It provides a framework for integrating health and social care services to ensure that older people can maintain functional ability, autonomy and well-being throughout the continuum of care.

The package outlines core interventions in three domains: health care, palliative care, and social care and support, including measures that recognize and address the needs of carers. It also identifies person-centred integrated care and education and training as key facilitating factors for effective implementation. Intended primarily for policy-makers and planners, the publication offers guidance on adapting LTC interventions to national contexts, strengthening coordination across sectors, engaging older people and carers in decision-making, and progressively building equitable, sustainable and integrated LTC systems aligned with healthy ageing and universal health coverage goals.

title: Achieving the targets for universal health coverage: how is Thailand monitoring progress?
authors: Woranan Witthayapipopsakul; Anond Kulthanmanusorn; Vuthiphan Vongmongkol; Shaheda Viriyathorn; Yaowaluk Wanwong; Viroj Tangcharoensathien
abstract: Universal health coverage (UHC) is one of the targets within the Sustainable Development Goalsthat the Member States of the United Nations have pledged to achieve by 2030. Target 3.8 has twomonitoring indicators: 3.8.1 for coverage of essential health services, for which a compound index from16 tracer indicators has recently been developed; and 3.8.2 for catastrophic expenditure on health.The global baseline monitoring of these two indicators in 2017 shows that the progress in many lowandmiddle-income countries is unlikely to be on track and achieved by 2030. The monitoring andevaluation mechanism for UHC progress is a crucial function to hold governments accountable andguide countries along their paths towards UHC. This paper outlines key monitoring and evaluationtools that Thailand uses to track UHC progress; compares the strengths and limitations of each tool;and discusses monitoring gaps and enabling factors related to development of the tools. Thailanduses several data sources to monitor three UHC dimensions: population coverage; service coverage;and financial risk protection. The four key sources are: (i) national surveys; (ii) health facility andadministrative data; (iii) specific disease registries; and (iv) research. Each source provides differentadvantages and is used concurrently to complement the others. Despite initially being developedto track progress for national health priorities, these tools are able to monitor most of the globalUHC indicators. Key enabling factors of Thai monitoring systems are a supportive infrastructure andinformation system; a policy requirement for routine patient data records; ownership and commitmentof the key responsible organizations; multisectoral collaboration; and sustainable in-country capacities.The areas for improvement are monitoring in the non-Thai population; tracking access to essentialmedicines; and maximizing the use of collected data. Lessons learnt from the Thai experience couldbe useful for other low- and middle-income countries in developing their UHC monitoring platforms.

abstract: Universal health coverage (UHC) is a key policy issue in countries of the WorldHealth Organization (WHO) South-East Asia Region. However, despite projectionsof significant increases in burden, there is little protection against the financial risksassociated with noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), including diabetes. Thailandachieved UHC of all 67 million of the population in 2002, under three public healthinsurance schemes. The country therefore provides a case-study on diabetesprevention and care in the context of UHC. Although the budget for the ThaiUniversal Coverage (UC) scheme, which covers nearly 80% of the population,increased significantly during 2003–2013, the proportion allocated to clinicalprevention and health promotion declined from 15% to 11%. The financial case forinvestment in diabetes prevention is made, particularly with respect to a focus onprimary care and the use of community volunteers. The UC scheme can expandto nearly 100% population coverage, with a comprehensive benefit packageand financial risk protection. Although the rates of complications and fatalitiesin patients with diabetes have improved over the last few years, achievementof well-controlled fasting blood glucose for all patients is still the main challengefor further improvement. It is recommended that, in order to improve coverageof diabetes care and prevention, it is essential for countries in the WHO SouthEast Asia Region to include major NCD services, in particular primary prevention,in their UHC strategies. Since a resilient health system is key to UHC delivery,strengthening of the health workforce and infrastructure should be part of anyaction plan to prevent and control diabetes

title: SEA/RC63/24 - Regional Strategy on Universal Health Coverage
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: There has been strong and consistent commitment to improving equity in health through universal coverage in the Region as well as at global level from WHO and Member States. An overall financing strategy towards achieving this goal has been developed for the Asia-Pacific Region jointly by the Regional Offices for South-East Asia and the Western-Pacific regions. Furthermore, these regional priorities will be the focus of the forthcoming 2010 World Health Report, “Financing for Universal Coverage”. The key challenges to financing for universal coverage in the Region are the high and potentially impoverishing out-of-pocket spending on health; a large and poor informal sector that is most vulnerable to the high cost of access to care; a large and mostly unregulated private sector that dominates provision of care; and the increasing burden of noncommunicable diseases requiring high-cost individual care. There are three choices in the progress towards universal coverage that health financing reform needs to consider: priority population to be reached with a chosen benefit package at a feasible public subsidy. A practical approach to shift from out-of-pocket payments towards equity and universal coverage is a step-by-step move, first to an intermediate stage of a mix of community initiatives to protect the informal sector and social insurance for the formal sector with general government revenues focusing on public health and the poor; and, to the next stage that consolidates community and social insurance into national-level social protection schemes with continued public investment in public health and target populations. In-depth technical assessments of the potential of this approach to sustainable financing for universal coverage in Member States is recommended for formulating a strategy for the Region to be considered by the Sixty-fourth Regional Committee in 2011 for further action. The High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting held in the Regional Office in New Delhi from 28 June to 1 July 2010 reviewed the working paper and made the following recommendations: Action by Member States • Evidence-based technical assessment should be carried out on financing for universal health coverage. Actions by WHO-SEARO (1) The Regional Office should provide support to Member States to carry out technical assessment on financing for universal health coverage. (2) A draft of the regional strategy on universal health coverage should be prepared through a series of consultative meetings and expert reviews. A regional consultation should also be organized to develop consensus on the regional strategy on universal health coverage. The working paper and the HLP recommendations based on it are submitted to the Sixty-third Session of the Regional Committee for its consideration. The Committee is also requested to consider the draft resolution on the subject.

title: Accelerating reforms of primary health care towards universal health coverage in Sri Lanka
authors: Susie Perera; Olivia Nieveras; Padmal de Silva; Chatura Wijesundara; Razia Pendse
abstract: Since the late 1920s, the Sri Lankan health system has been based on a firm foundation of primaryhealth care, and it has been recognized internationally as a highly successful low-cost model.However, rethinking the future health-care model has been essential, owing to the country havingone of the fastest ageing populations in the world, coupled with a high premature mortality fromnoncommunicable diseases. To sustain past gains and meet new challenges, several models centredon an expanded primary health-care system have been trialled and refined in the past decade. Primaryhealth care was identified as a key priority in the National Health Strategic Master Plan 2016–2025,and in 2018 the Cabinet approved the Policy on healthcare delivery for universal health coverage.This policy introduces the “shared care cluster” system, whereby an apex specialist institution servesthe local primary care referral institutions. The catchment population is divided into populations ofapproximately 5000, for which one family doctor is responsible. Strengthening and retaining humanresources at these primary-level curative institutions will be essential, especially in rural locations.Also critical will be initiatives to orient the population’s health-seeking behaviours. Sustained politicalcommitment, an effective communication strategy, a tailored health workforce policy, performancemonitoring and evaluation, coordination mechanisms, and changes in administrative and financialregulations are some of the future factors that will be critical to realizing the full potential of primaryhealth care and accelerating universal health coverage in Sri Lanka.

title: Universal health coverage and the health Sustainable Development Goal: achievements and challenges for Sri Lanka
authors: Amala de Silva; Thushara Ranasinghe; Palitha Abeykoon
abstract: With state-funded health care that is free at the point of delivery, a sound primaryhealth-care policy and widespread health-care services, Sri Lanka seems a goodexample of universal health coverage. Yet, health transition and disparities inprovision and financing threaten this situation. Sri Lanka did well on the MillenniumDevelopment Goal health indicators, but the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)for health has a wider purview, which is to “ensure healthy lives and promote wellbeing for all at all ages”. The gender gap in life expectancy and the gap betweenlife expectancy and healthy life expectancy make achievement of the health SDGmore challenging. Although women and children do well overall, the comparativehealth disadvantage for men in Sri Lanka is a cause for concern. From a financingperspective, high out-of-pocket expenditure and high utilization of the private sector,even by those in the lowest income quintile, are concerns, as is the emerging “thirdtier”, where some individuals accessing state health care that is free at the pointof delivery actually bear some of the costs of drugs, investigations and surgery.This cost sharing is resulting in catastrophic health expenditure for individuals,and delays in and non-compliance with treatment. These concerns about provisionand financing must be addressed, as health transition will intensify the morbidityburden and loss of well-being, and could derail plans to achieve the health SDG.

title: Tracking universal health coverage: 2023 global monitoring report: executive summary
authors: World Health Organization; International Bank for Reconstruction and Development; The World Bank
abstract:
This executive summary synthesizes the main findings of the global monitoring report on progress towards universal health coverage (UHC) within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals. Based on the latest available data from WHO and the World Bank, it examines trends in two core dimensions: coverage of essential health services and financial protection, measured through out-of-pocket health spending. It is intended to inform policy-makers and stakeholders on the current status of UHC and priority areas for action.

The summary highlights that global progress towards UHC has stalled since 2015, with limited improvements in service coverage and increasing levels of financial hardship. While gains in service coverage were observed between 2000 and 2021, these have slowed considerably in recent years, and substantial inequalities persist both within and between countries. At the same time, the number of people facing catastrophic or impoverishing health expenditures has increased, disproportionately affecting lower-income populations. The COVID-19 pandemic has further disrupted health services and weakened financial protection. The findings underscore the need for accelerated policy action, increased public investment, and a stronger primary health care approach to expand equitable access to services and reduce financial barriers to care.

abstract:
This executive summary presents the main findings of the global monitoring report on progress towards universal health coverage (UHC) within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals. At the same time, the incidence of catastrophic health spending increased, and a large share of the population continued to experience financial hardship. Persistent inequalities in both service coverage and financial protection are observed across and within countries. The pandemic has disrupted essential health services and is likely to exacerbate financial barriers to care. The findings highlight the need for strengthened primary health care–oriented systems, increased public investment, and improved data and monitoring capacities to support equitable and sustainable progress towards UHC.

title: Handbook for conducting assessments of barriers to effective coverage with health services: in support of equity-oriented reforms towards universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This handbook provides methodological guidance for conducting assessments of barriers to effective coverage with health services in support of equity-oriented reforms towards universal health coverage. Developed by WHO, it supports national and subnational authorities, researchers and partners in identifying supply- and demand-side barriers that affect equitable access to quality health services across the continuum of care. The publication is grounded in the Tanahashi framework for effective coverage and adopts a mixed methods approach combining key informant interviews, literature reviews, quantitative analyses and focus group discussions. It also integrates concepts related to health equity, progressive universalism, primary health care, human rights and social determinants of health.

The document outlines practical steps for planning, implementing, analysing and reporting barriers assessments, including adaptations for humanitarian contexts. It presents tools, frameworks and templates to support evidence synthesis, stakeholder engagement and the translation of findings into policy dialogue and health systems strengthening efforts. Emphasis is placed on understanding barriers experienced by disadvantaged populations in order to reduce inequities, improve service coverage and inform equity-oriented reforms towards universal health coverage.

title: Global oral health status report: towards universal health coverage for oral health by 2030: executive summary
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This executive summary presents the main findings of the WHO Global oral health status report and provides an overview of the global burden of oral diseases, associated inequalities and the challenges to achieving universal health coverage for oral health by 2030. Drawing on the latest available evidence from the Global Burden of Disease project, the International Agency for Research on Cancer and WHO surveys, it describes the prevalence and distribution of major oral diseases, their shared social determinants and risk factors with other noncommunicable diseases, and their substantial health, social and economic impacts. The report also introduces country oral health profiles to support monitoring and future action.

The publication outlines opportunities to reorient oral health systems from predominantly restorative care towards prevention, health promotion and integration within primary health care and universal health coverage. It highlights the need to strengthen oral health services, workforce capacity, surveillance, research and access to essential interventions while addressing persistent inequalities affecting disadvantaged populations. The report serves as a baseline resource for implementing the WHO Global Strategy on Oral Health and the Global Oral Health Action Plan, supporting Member States in monitoring progress and advancing equitable oral health for all by 2030.

title: Strengthening primary health care as a key element towards achieving universal health coverage
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: Comprehensive primary health care (CPHC) is widely recognized as an inclusive, effective and efficient approach for achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and the health-related SDGs; a cornerstone for promoting health security through the provision of essential public health functions; and the foundation for sustainable and integrated people-centred health care. The UN High-Level Meeting on UHC, scheduled in New York in September 2023, through an anticipated Political Declaration by Heads of State and Governments, is expected to further enhance global commitment and momentum towards health for all through strengthened focus on primary health care (PHC). The South-East Asia Regional Strategy on Primary Health Care 2022–2030 (or the SE Asia Regional PHC Strategy), developed in consultation with South-East Asia Region Member States and partners and endorsed during the Seventy-fifth session of the Regional Committee, provides a unified framework for strengthening PHC as a foundation for achievement of UHC and the SDGs. The SE Asia Region PHC Strategy was guided by and aligns with key regional and global documents, particularly resolution SEA/RC74/R1. Moreover, as requested by the Seventy-fifth Regional Committee, the South-East Asia Regional Forum for PHC-oriented Health Systems (hereinafter also referred to as the SE Asia Regional Forum) was established as a government-led initiative to promote knowledge and experience sharing and synergized support from partners in tackling specific bottle necks for PHC strengthening in the Region. While there has been notable progress across Member States towards PHC-orientation of health systems, including in recent years, focused attention is required in the following areas: capacities to track and monitor progress and promote accountability; institutionalize and strengthen participatory mechanisms in UHC/PHC governance; strengthen knowledge management mechanisms to scale up and contextualize effective and cost-efficient models; and promote synergized support from WHO and partners tailored to national systems and context, especially in tackling implementation bottlenecks. Improving quality, integration of disease control programmes particularly NCDs, ensuring continuum of care across the life course and levels of care, integration of public health functions, developing multidisciplinary teams to provide PHC, and leveraging digital health for people-centred PHC are some of the common challenges that countries in the Region face with regard to PHC.This Working Paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. The HLP reviewed the paper and made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy-sixth Session of the Regional Committee:Action by Member StatesParticipate in the preparation of the Roundtable and development of the Ministerial Declaration, including the virtual consultation and discussions at the second meeting of the SEAR PHC Forum.Actions by WHOInclude comments from Member States to further highlight the significance of key recommended topics in the technical report to the Seventy-sixth Session of the Regional Committee for South-East Asia and the discussion stated above, including investment and financing for PHC, linkages between PHC and other levels of health care, digital health and telemedicine, PHC infrastructure, climate change resilience and traditional medicine.Facilitate discussions, under the leadership of the Government of India as the host country, among Member States to prepare and develop the Ministerial Declaration for smooth adoption through consensus at the Roundtable.This Working Paper and the HLP Meeting recommendations are presented to the Seventy-sixth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration and decision.

title: WHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening

abstract:
This WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of digital interventions to strengthen health systems and support progress towards universal health coverage (UHC). Developed in response to the growing adoption of digital technologies and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on digital health, it addresses the need for rigorous evaluation of digital health interventions to ensure that investments are informed by evidence of their benefits, harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource implications and equity considerations. The guideline emphasizes that digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, the fundamental components of well-functioning health systems.

The recommendations focus on a prioritized set of digital health interventions accessible at a minimum through mobile devices, including birth and death notification, stock notification and commodity management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, digital tracking of clients’ health status and services, health worker decision support, and digital learning for health workers. The guideline also outlines implementation considerations, identifies research gaps, and supports ministries of health, public health practitioners, development partners and other stakeholders in making evidence-based decisions on the adoption, scale-up and institutionalization of effective digital health interventions.

The review examines governance and leadership, service delivery, health financing, health information systems, workforce capacity, risk communication and community engagement, emergency preparedness, and research related to refugee and migrant health. Using a qualitative methodology based on desk review, stakeholder consultations and field visits, the assessment explores how refugee and migrant health services are integrated into the national health system and identifies opportunities for strengthening long-term resilience.

The report finds that Estonia provides refugees and migrants with broad access to health services through existing legal and institutional frameworks, including health insurance coverage and primary health care. At the same time, challenges remain, including shortages of family physicians and other health professionals, language and communication barriers, limited collection of migration-specific health data, difficulties navigating the health system, and gaps in community outreach and emergency preparedness. The review highlights areas for improvement in coordination, service accessibility, workforce development, health information management and research, and proposes actions to support equitable access to care and strengthen health system responsiveness for both refugee and migrant populations and host communities.

This report presents a joint review of Uganda’s refugee and migrant health system conducted by the World Health Organization, the Ministry of Health of Uganda and key international partners. The review examines the capacity of the national health system to respond to the health needs of refugees, migrants and host communities, within the context of Uganda’s long-standing policy of refugee inclusion and its commitment to integrating refugee services into national systems. Using a combination of desk review, stakeholder consultations and field visits, the assessment explores health system governance, service delivery, financing, health information systems, workforce capacity, emergency preparedness, health promotion and research.

The analysis highlights achievements in providing refugees and migrants with access to essential health services, including communicable disease control, immunization, maternal and child health care, and emergency response mechanisms. At the same time, it identifies persistent challenges, including shortages of health workers, recurrent stockouts of medicines and vaccines, limited financing, gaps in mental health services, barriers related to communication and cultural mediation, and weaknesses in health information management. The report outlines opportunities for strengthening health system resilience, improving service integration, enhancing preparedness and ensuring equitable access to quality health care for refugees, migrants and host populations in Uganda.

title: WHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening: executive summary
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This executive summary presents the principal recommendations of the WHO guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, developed to provide evidence-based normative guidance on the use of digital technologies to support progress towards universal health coverage. Produced in response to growing investment in digital health and the need for rigorous evaluation of its benefits and limitations, the guideline critically assesses the evidence for prioritized digital health interventions, considering their effectiveness, potential harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource implications and equity. It emphasizes that digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, the fundamental components of well-functioning health systems.

The guideline focuses on a prioritized set of digital interventions accessible at a minimum through mobile devices, including birth and death notification, stock notification and commodity management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, digital tracking of patients’ health status and services, health worker decision support, and digital learning for health workers. It highlights the importance of implementing these interventions within an enabling ICT and health system environment and provides recommendations and implementation considerations to support informed decision-making by ministries of health, public health practitioners, development partners and other organizations investing in digital health.

abstract: In 2025, the fourth year of the full-scale war, continued attacks on health care, repeated displacement and harsh winter conditions driven by damage to energy and civilian infrastructure put Ukraine’s health system under unprecedented pressure. Communities living close to the front line faced acute trauma needs and fragile referral pathways, while gaps in continuity of care for noncommunicable and infectious diseases elevated outbreak risks and left millions coping with mental health challenges and war-related injuries requiring rehabilitation. Working alongside the Ministry of Health and partners, WHO reached 1.9 million people by reinforcing emergency medical services and trauma care, sustaining primary health care through outreach to hard-to-reach areas and strengthening surveillance, laboratory capacity and preparedness for epidemic and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks. WHO delivered essential medicines, supplies and equipment to health facilities, installed modular units to restore service capacity where infrastructure was damaged, supported medical evacuations and helped facilities stay functional during power outages through heating and water stations. title: Health facility resilience
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract:
This agenda item positions resilient health facilities as essential to health security and universal health coverage in the WHO SE Asia Region. Health facilities should be safe for patients and health workers and be capable of surging critical services and continuity of essential services following emergencies irrespective of the type and confluence of emergency hazard risks that SE Asia Region Member States typically and increasingly face. This Working Paper applies an all-hazards risk-based approach for health facility resilience and proposes four linked attributes that are required for resilience – safety, sustainability, smartness and support. Safe facilities are those that structurally withstand emergency shocks and function with agility and additional capacity to deliver emergency surge response while providing uninterrupted essential services. Sustainable facilities withstand the vagaries of climate change and are of low-carbon impact as well as appropriate to the local environment. Smart facilities incorporate cost-effective health, information and communication technologies, are connected, data-driven, and enabled by evidence and innovation. Supported facilities are routinely monitored, assessed and maintained, with earmarked financing and accountable governance mechanisms that are embedded in national health systems and health security frameworks. Although Member States have policy mandates, technical tools and country need and experience, national status of resilience of health facilities is uneven. Building codes are not updated to account for current risks and climate hazards, and enforcement of compliance to existing codes is not rigorous. Furthermore, assessments are often one-off with recommendations unimplemented; lifelines and supply chains remain fragile; maintenance and refurbishment non-systematic; adoption and upgrading of health, information and communication technology and innovation inadequate; financing is ad hoc; and accountability frameworks and mechanisms sub-optimal.
The agenda, therefore, calls for an articulated and comprehensive regional framework and resolution on multi-hazard risk-prioritized, financed and institutionalized health facility resilience to be implemented with agreed accountability mechanisms across all Member States. The Secretariat proposed an approach within the realms of established global and regional mandates, including the Fourteenth General Programme of Work, the Male’ Declaration, regional resilience roadmaps and the Banyan Framework for Health and Well-being in the WHO South-East Asia Region (2026–2028). It illustrated current notable practices through Nepal’s nationally adapted Hospital Safety Index Plus approach and Thailand’s hospital safety assessments, while outlining the uneven status of resilience across Member States due to the multiple systemic, technical and operational challenges. The proposed response is a systematic regional approach based on ‘Safe, Sustainable, Smart and Supported’ facilities, or 4S. It was proposed that Member States would prioritize facilities by risk and service role, institutionalize periodic all-hazards risk assessments, convert findings into costed investment plans, secure reliable lifelines, strengthen climate, heat and cyber preparedness, ensure surge response and protect essential health care continuity, engage and enhance capacity of multidisciplinary teams, finance resilience and monitor progress and build accountability and solidarity. The presentation concluded by seeking Regional Committee endorsement, sustained domestic and external investment, and a concise regional indicator set on health facility resilience reported through existing mechanisms to support measurable and accountable progress by 2030. The agenda item was deliberated at length by the High-Level Preparatory Meeting. The HLP Meeting reviewed the Agenda and made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee: 
Actions by Member States
(1) Endorse and operationalize a regional approach based on four linked attributes: Safe, Sustainable, Smart and Supported health facilities, and further support the drafting and consideration of a Regional Committee resolution on multi-hazard risk-informed health facility resilience, with a time-bound objective to assess and progressively upgrade priority health facilities by 2030.
(2) Conduct periodic all-hazards risk assessments using the regionally upgraded and country contextualized WHO Hospital Safety Index assessment tool, the Strategic Toolkit for Assessing Risks – Systems and Health Facilities, climate-resilience and other relevant assessment tools, linked and synergized for ease of operational implementation. Apply these across relevant levels of care, including private facilities where appropriate, and translate findings into prioritized plans factoring in capital, retrofitting and maintenance costs; preparedness and readiness for emergency care surge response and essential service-continuity.
(3) Ensure reliable clean energy, water, sanitation, hygiene, health care waste management and infection prevention and control; essential diagnostics, medicines and medical logistics including oxygen; communications, transport, supply chains and patient referral and safety mechanisms. Strengthen climate, heat and cyber preparedness; digital connectivity and workforce capacity tested by drills; and embed resilience in policies, standards, licensing, universal health coverage and health security plans, supported by ring-fenced domestic and external financing. 
Actions by WHO
(1) Support the preparation and, subject to Regional Committee guidance, implementation of the proposed resolution. Provide regionally adapted standards, technical packages and assessment tools for Safe, Sustainable, Smart and Supported health facilities, including guidance on prioritization based on multi-hazard risk and service demand and enhanced application across public and private health facilities enabled by regulatory and incentive mechanisms.
(2) Assist Member States to undertake assessments, prepare costed investment plans, strengthen infrastructure and lifelines, establish maintenance systems, improve digital and referral networks, reinforce emergency coordination, and train and test multidisciplinary teams and institution of regulatory, incentivization and accountability mechanisms. Facilitate regional exchange of evidence, innovations, model health facility designs and standards and scalable practices.
(3) Develop, in tandem with Member States, a concise and tiered regional indicator framework on health facility resilience status and periodic regional snapshot/profile, aligned with existing International Health Regulations (2005), Universal Health Coverage and climate-health monitoring mechanisms. The Working Paper along with the HLP Meeting recommendations are placed before the Seventy-ninth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration, as appropriate.

title: Closing the gap to end TB: Strategic priorities for the WHO South-East Asia Region
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract:
Tuberculosis remains a major public health and development challenge in the WHO South-East Asia Region and continues to account for the largest share of the global burden. In 2024, the Region reported an estimated 3.68 million incident tuberculosis cases and 433 000 deaths, underscoring the urgency of accelerating implementation of the End TB Strategy and related regional commitments.
Recent progress is encouraging but insufficient. Since 2015, the Region has reduced tuberculosis incidence by 16% and deaths by 23%, while treatment coverage and treatment success have both exceeded 85% in many settings. These gains reflect strong programme recovery, expanded case finding and sustained efforts by Member States, but they remain below the milestones required to end tuberculosis as a public health problem.
Important challenges continue to slow progress, including delayed diagnosis, a substantial burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, persistent catastrophic costs for affected households, and financing levels that remain well below estimated need.
The strategic priorities for the Region are to accelerate earlier and more complete case detection, expand targeted prevention and active case finding, improve treatment quality and adherence support, strengthen integration within primary health care and universal health coverage reforms, and reinforce multisectoral action, community engagement and sustainable financing. Early preparedness for the introduction of new tuberculosis vaccines should also be advanced as a strategic regional priority.
This Working Paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. The HLP Meeting reviewed the paper, deliberated in detail on the Agenda, and made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy ninth Session of the Regional Committee:
Actions by Member States
(1) Accelerate the adoption and scale-up of updated WHO recommendations on diagnostics, treatment, tuberculosis preventive treatment and active case-finding, prioritizing high-risk and underserved populations.
(2) Protect essential tuberculosis services and strengthen domestic financing, social protection and community-based support to reduce catastrophic costs for affected households, while addressing barriers to access such as stigma and discrimination.
(3) Advance multisectoral action, service integration and early preparedness for new tuberculosis vaccines, including planning for regulatory, delivery, financing and post-introduction monitoring. 
Actions by WHO
(1) Provide technical support for the rapid implementation of WHO-recommended diagnostics, targeted active case-finding among vulnerable groups, treatment regimens, preventive interventions, digital tools and differentiated service-delivery models, while helping countries reduce barriers to accessing tuberculosis services, such as stigma and discrimination.
(2) Support countries to use epidemiological, programme and modelling evidence to prioritize high-impact interventions, improve efficiency and protect gains in case detection, treatment and prevention.
(3) Facilitate regional collaboration, partner coordination and resource mobilization for integrated tuberculosis responses, including vaccine readiness, community engagement and action on social determinants. The Working Paper, along with the recommendations of the High-Level Preparatory Meeting, is placed before the Seventy-ninth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration, as appropriate. In line with the recommendation of the High-Level Preparatory Meeting, the Regional Committee may also wish to consider adopting a resolution to sustain political commitment, guide implementation of the strategic priorities and strengthen accountability for follow-up by Member States, WHO and partners.

title: Annual report on monitoring progress on UHC and health-related SDGs
authors: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract:
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development sets out 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to be achieved by 2030, underpinned by the principle of ‘leaving no one behind’. At its core, SDG3 aims to ‘ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages’. In 2016, the Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly adopted resolution WHA69.11, Health in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, urging Member States to strengthen health systems, advance universal health coverage (UHC), promote multisectoral action, and monitor progress towards the health and health-related SDGs. In response, the Seventieth session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia in 2017 requested the Regional Director to present an annual report on monitoring progress on UHC and other health and health-related SDGs as a substantive agenda item until 2030. In addition to reviewing regional progress towards UHC and other health and health-related SDGs, each annual report includes a thematic chapter on an area of strategic importance to Member States. In its eleventh edition, the annual report presents a thematic chapter on ‘Leveraging Climate Change Monitoring for Public Health Action’ in the WHO SE Asia Region. It brings into focus the imperative need to strengthen climate-informed surveillance, climate-resilient health systems and multisectoral action to address the growing impact of climate-sensitive health risks on population health and health system performance. The Secretariat highlighted continued regional progress towards UHC (SDG 3.8) and other health and health-related SDGs, with the UHC Service Coverage Index (SDG 3.8.1) for the Region increasing from 53 in 2010 to 68 in 2023, alongside improvements in maternal and child health, immunization and malaria control. Progress on financial hardship (SDG 3.8.2) was noted as directionally positive (30.9% of the regional population faced financial hardship from out-of-pocket (OOP) health spending in 2022 compared with 41.4% in 2000). However, it is insufficient and uneven: the persistently high absolute burden remains one of the Region’s most critical challenges on the path to UHC by 2030. Persistent challenges include an unrelenting burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), tuberculosis, health workforce shortages and inequities in access to quality health services. The Secretariat emphasized the need for accelerated actions to reposition primary health care (PHC) as the foundation of UHC and health security, to invest in quality of care, not just coverage, and to scale up NCDs prevention and management, ensuring continuity of care through PHC and sustained financing for chronic disease management.
Key interventions are also necessary to strengthen publicly funded, compulsory prepaid coverage to reduce financial hardship and lower OOP health spending, particularly on medicines; to build a future-ready health workforce and pursue a safe, equitable, data-driven, AI-enabled digital transformation of health systems; and to adopt a multisectoral, whole-of-government approach that institutionalizes health in all policies and building climate-resilient, sustainable health systems. This Working Paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. The HLP Meeting reviewed the paper, deliberated in detail on the agenda, and made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee: 
Actions by Member States
(1) Strengthen PHC to accelerate progress towards UHC and the other health and health-related SDGs, with particular emphasis on quality of care, NCD prevention and management, healthy ageing and equitable access to essential health services.
(2) Strengthen sustainable health financing mechanisms to improve financial protection, reduce out-of-pocket expenditure and expand equitable access to affordable health services, medicines and health technologies.
(3) Strengthen health information systems, health workforce capacity, climate-resilient health systems, accelerate digital transformation and improve multisectoral collaboration to improve monitoring and implementation of UHC and the health-related SDGs. 
Actions by WHO
(1) Continue providing technical support to strengthen the monitoring of UHC and health-related SDGs, health information systems, the digital transformation of the health system, national health accounts and the integration of climate and health monitoring indicators.
(2) Support Member States in strengthening PHC, health financing, workforce capacity, climate-resilient health systems, regional knowledge exchange and resource mobilization.
(3) Facilitate regional collaboration and sharing of country experiences and good practices to accelerate implementation of evidence-based interventions towards achieving UHC and the health-related SDGs by 2030. This Working Paper along with the HLP Meeting recommendations are placed before the Seventy-ninth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration

title: Accelerating digital transformation of health systems: Establishment of the South-East Asia digital health and artificial intelligence collaborative network (SEA-DAC)
authors: World Health Organization. Country Office for South Africa
abstract:
Digital transformation of health systems is a critical accelerator of universal health coverage (UHC) and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The Global Initiative on Digital Health (GIDH), launched by the World Health Organization in February 2024 as a WHO-managed ‘network of networks’, provides the global framework to align resources with country-led digital transformation, reduce duplication and fragmentation, and strengthen knowledge exchange. Member States in the South-East Asia Region have made considerable progress in advancing national digital health strategies, telemedicine, health information systems, digital public infrastructure (DPI) and early applications of artificial intelligence (AI). However, regional collaboration remains fragmented and largely ad hoc. Formal requests from Member States for structured peer learning and technology cooperation, together with standing offers of financial and technical support under GIDH, have been slowed by case-by-case bilateral coordination, underscoring the need for a dedicated, Member State-led regional mechanism. This Working Paper proposes the establishment of the South-East Asia Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence Collaborative Network (SEA-DAC) as the dedicated regional implementation arm of GIDH. SEA-DAC would operate as a voluntary, consensus-based network of national agencies responsible for digital health and AI for health, governed by an Assembly of Members, a Steering Group, technical Working Groups and national focal points, supported by a WHO-SEARO Secretariat. Its design adopts validated practices from established global and regional mechanisms and is explicitly framed to complement, and not duplicate, existing partnerships, with technical delivery operationalized through WHO project collaboration agreements.
This Working Paper was presented to the High-Level Preparatory (HLP) Meeting for its review and recommendations. The HLP Meeting reviewed the paper, deliberated on the agenda item, and made the following recommendations for consideration by the Seventy-ninth Session of the Regional Committee: 
Actions by Member States
(1) Support the establishment of the South-East Asia Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence Collaborative Network (SEA-DAC) by the Regional Committee and, subject to endorsement, designate a national agency for digital health and nominate a senior representative and national focal points for its governance and technical work.
(2) Identify and share national priorities, technical expertise, digital public goods and adaptable solutions that can contribute to peer learning, technology cooperation and early SEA-DAC deliverables.
(3) Contribute actively to the governance, workplan and sustainable financing of SEA-DAC, while upholding equity, national sovereignty, responsible AI and complementarity with existing mechanisms. 
Actions by WHO
(1) Subject to the Regional Committee’s endorsement and subsequent action as per the recommendations for Member States, convene the inaugural Assembly of Members of the Network.
(2) Present the draft terms of reference and governance documents for consideration and adoption, as appropriate, by the inaugural Assembly of Members, and facilitate the establishment of the initial working groups and a results-oriented workplan.
(3) Propose sustainable and transparent financing, due diligence, conflict-of-interest stipulations, monitoring and reporting arrangements, and priority early outputs for the Network. The Working Paper, together with the recommendations of the HLP Meeting, is placed before the Seventy-ninth Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia for its consideration and decision.

The meeting aimed to update countries on global, regional and national developments; facilitate access to technical and financial support mechanisms; and provide a platform for sharing experiences, challenges and good practices. Participants included national AMR and IPC focal points, representatives from WHO, the European Commission, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control and partner institutions. Discussions highlighted persistent barriers such as limited funding, workforce shortages, gaps in surveillance – particularly in long-term care facilities – and low public awareness. Countries presented tools and approaches to enhance stewardship, accountability and data driven monitoring. The meeting also included a consultation on the development of a new AMR Accountability Index to benchmark national progress and strengthen transparency. Overall, the event reinforced regional collaboration, mobilized resources and advanced collective efforts to accelerate AMR NAP implementation across the WHO European Region.

title: WHO guidance for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: why it matters
authors: Adhikari, TB; Rashidi, MM; Alupo, P; Cieza, A; Rylance, S
abstract:
Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease affect more than 500 million people worldwide and remain major causes of preventable morbidity and mortality, with the greatest burden falling on low- and middle-income countries because of persistent inequities in access to diagnosis, essential inhaled medicines and quality primary care. This editorial explains why updated WHO guidance for the management of these conditions in primary care is needed, highlighting the limitations of existing global policy tools and the need to align recommendations with current evidence, essential medicines and universal health coverage commitments.

The article outlines the principles underpinning WHO guideline development, including transparent methods, systematic evidence reviews, multidisciplinary and geographically diverse expert participation, and consideration of feasibility, equity and resource implications. It emphasizes that forthcoming WHO guidelines, expected in 2027, are intended to complement existing clinical guidelines by providing policy-oriented recommendations that are applicable across diverse health-system contexts, particularly resource-constrained settings. The guidance aims to support national decisions on diagnosis, treatment, referral and follow-up, inform essential medicines lists and clinical protocols, and strengthen the integration of chronic respiratory disease management into routine primary health care, while recognizing that successful implementation will depend on country adaptation and sustained investment in health systems.

title: Palliative care in humanitarian responses
authors: Kaade H; Muehlensiepen, F; Rosa, WE; Heinze, M; Kamp, M; Allsop MJ
abstract:
Humanitarian health responses should be evaluated not only by their ability to save lives but also by their capacity to relieve serious health-related suffering. This perspective argues that palliative care is an essential component of quality humanitarian health care rather than an optional or specialist service, and that it should be systematically integrated into preparedness, emergency response and recovery. Drawing on existing WHO guidance, humanitarian standards and implementation experience, the authors identify persistent barriers to integration, including limited access to essential medicines, service delivery models focused exclusively on acute stabilization, workforce constraints, insufficient leadership and accountability, and misconceptions about the role of palliative care.

The article proposes a practical operational framework to support implementation across humanitarian settings, encompassing policy and leadership, workforce development, reliable access to essential medicines, integration into clinical pathways, family and caregiver support, and continuous quality improvement. It emphasizes that effective palliative care depends on systems rather than individual improvisation and that relief of suffering should be embedded within routine humanitarian health services alongside life-saving interventions. Strengthening these system components can improve quality of care, support families and communities, reduce moral distress among health workers and ensure that humanitarian responses consistently uphold dignity and compassionate care.

title: Policy considerations to improve access to refractive error care
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of vision impairment worldwide. Although spectacles are a simple and cost-effective solution, barriers such as high costs, restrictive regulations, workforce shortages, limited public sector involvement and poor awareness continue to limit access, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This guide supports policy-makers, lawmakers and regulatory authorities in identifying legislative and regulatory barriers affecting the provision of refractive error care and considering policy actions to improve access and affordability.

Aligned with the WHO SPECS 2030 initiative, the guide focuses on five policy areas: improving access to refractive error services through integration of spectacles dispensing and screening programmes; building workforce capacity through competency-based teams, strengthened training systems and appropriate engagement of informal providers; increasing public awareness of myopia risk factors; reducing costs through tax and tariff reforms, streamlined importation procedures and stronger distribution systems; and strengthening quality, surveillance and research through national standards and integration of refractive error indicators into health information systems. The guide emphasizes government leadership, cross-sectoral collaboration and stakeholder engagement to improve equitable access to refractive error care and support progress towards universal health coverage.

title: WHO contribution in Somalia 2020-2025: evaluation report

This independent evaluation report assesses the contribution of the World Health Organization (WHO) in Somalia during 2020–2025 in relation to national health priorities, the WHO Country Cooperation Strategy (2021–2025), the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and WHO global strategic agendas. Conducted within the context of Somalia’s protracted humanitarian crisis, insecurity, climate shocks and fragile health system, the evaluation examines WHO’s role in advancing universal health coverage, strengthening health security, promoting healthier populations and reinforcing health governance and partnerships. Using mixed methods, including document review, interviews, focus group discussions and stakeholder surveys, the report analyses the relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency and sustainability of WHO-supported interventions.

The report highlights WHO’s contributions to immunization, disease surveillance, outbreak preparedness and emergency response, as well as its technical leadership in policy development and coordination. It also identifies persistent challenges related to fragmented funding, weak monitoring systems, limited subnational ownership and dependence on humanitarian financing. The evaluation outlines lessons learned and provides recommendations to strengthen strategic planning, equity-oriented programming, health system resilience, coordination and sustainable financing to support more inclusive and durable health outcomes in Somalia.

title: Ending the neglect to attain the sustainable development goals: noma control: technical brief
authors: World Health Organization
abstract:
This technical brief provides an evidence-based overview of noma to support implementation of the WHO road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021–2030 following the disease’s inclusion in the WHO list of neglected tropical diseases in 2023. It describes the epidemiology, clinical progression and risk factors associated with noma, a rapidly progressing gangrenous disease that primarily affects young children living in conditions of extreme poverty, malnutrition and poor hygiene. The document highlights the disease burden, challenges related to surveillance and reporting, and the social consequences experienced by affected individuals, including disability, stigma and discrimination.

The publication outlines strategic interventions for noma control, including early detection, case management, improvements in water, sanitation and hygiene, nutritional support, oral health care, community awareness and integration into national health systems. It presents the global target of disease control together with indicators and milestones for monitoring progress towards 2030, and describes the methodology used to develop disease maps, establish targets and support routine data collection. The brief serves as a reference for countries, partners and WHO teams in planning, implementing and monitoring integrated, multisectoral interventions for noma control.
